common_complications: Failure of the graft to heal, narrowing of the ear canal, scarring or adhesion's in the middle ear, hearing loss, dislocation of the prosthesis or facial nerve injury. The surgery can result in post-operative pain and/or infection. Patients can infrequently have bad reactions to anesthesia.

name: Stapedectomy (removal of middle ear bone)
description: During a stapedectomy the surgeon removes the innermost bone (stapes) of the three bones (the stapes, the incus, and the malleus) of the middle ear. The removed bone is replaced with a small plastic tube surrounding a short length of stainless steel wire. This procedure is performed to improve hearing loss that results from abnormal bone growth of the stapes (otosclerosis).
common_complications: Complications include: increased hearing loss, vertigo (room spinning), damage to the other bones of the middle ear, facial nerve damage, perforated ear drum, temporary loss of taste, ringing in the ears (tinnitus), and infection. Occasionally the adverse effects are serious enough to require repeat surgery. Patients can infrequently have bad reactions to anesthesia.

name: Cochlear implant (implanted hearing device)
description: A surgical procedure involving the implantation of an electronic hearing device that helps produce hearing sensations in patients with severe hearing loss. The person wears a device behind the ear that picks up sounds and sends signals to the implanted device.
common_complications: Complications may include: facial nerve damage, cerebrospinal fluid leakage, dizziness or vertigo, ringing in the ears (tinnitus), taste disturbances, numbness, and infection. Patients can infrequently have bad reactions to anesthesia.

name: Myringotomy and tympanostomy (ear tubes)
description: The surgeon makes a small incision in the eardrum (tympanic membrane) to drain fluid. Most of the time a small tube (tympanoplasty tube) will be placed to prevent the fluid from re-accumulating. The most common cause of the fluid buildup is a chronic middle ear infection (otitis media).
common_complications: Complications include: persistent ear infection, thickening of the eardrum, persistent perforation after the tube falls out, chronic ear drainage, scarring of the eardrum, abnormal reaction to the tube, and infection. Patients can infrequently have bad reactions to anesthesia.

name: Deviated septum (septoplasty)
description: Surgical repair of a deviated septum is called a septoplasty. The surgery consists of removing, reshaping and repositioning the septum back to the center of the nose. The surgery is performed when the deviated septum causes frequent sinus infections, obstructive breathing, noisy breathing or frequent nosebleeds.
common_complications: Perforated septum, the need for a repeat surgery, and infection. Patients can infrequently have bad reactions to anesthesia.

name: Tonsillectomy (removal of tonsils)
description: Tonsillectomy is a surgical procedure to remove the tonsils. The tonsils are removed because of chronic infection, and also to relieve the obstruction in obstructive sleep apnea. Many times the adenoids are removed as well (adenoidectomy).
common_complications: Bleeding after surgery, injury to the soft palate and uvula, and infection. Patients can infrequently have bad reactions to the general anesthesia including allergic reactions.

name: Grommet removal (eardrum tube removal)
description: A grommet is another name for a tympanoplasty tube. The tubes are usually removed after a year if they do not fall out on their own. The tubes are placed to drain fluid from the middle ear.
common_complications: Rarely damage to the eardrum or infection.

name: Grommet insertion (eardrum tube insertion)
description: A grommet is another name for a tympanoplasty tube. These tubes are placed in the eardrum to remove trapped fluid in the middle ear. The most common cause of the fluid accumulation is a chronic infection. The fluid causes hearing problems and sometimes dizziness. The tubes are usually left in for one year. Or the tube may come out on its own with healing of the eardrum.
common_complications: Damage to the eardrum. All surgery comes with the risk of infection and blood clots. Patients can infrequently have bad reactions to the general anesthesia including allergic reactions.

name: KUB (x-ray of abdomen)
description: A KUB is an abdominal x-ray usually performed to look for intestinal blockage, free air (air that has escaped from the intestine because of a bowel perforation) or proper placement of a nasogastric (nose to stomach) tube.
common_complications: A KUB requires only a small amount of radiation and is considered a safe procedure.

name: Renal ultrasound (kidney ultrasound)
description: An ultrasound (sonogram) consists of high frequency sound waves. A renal ultrasound is done to evaluate the kidney's size, position, and shape. The test can help diagnose kidney stones, tumors, and cysts. A Doppler ultrasound exam may also be performed to evaluate blood flow to the kidneys.
common_complications: None

name: Scrotal ultrasound (ultrasound of contents of testicle sac)
description: An ultrasound (sonogram) consists of high frequency sound waves. A scrotal ultrasound can detect fluid collections, cysts, tumors and inflammation. A Doppler ultrasound exam may also be performed to evaluate blood flow to the testes. This is a good test to help diagnose testicular torsion (a twisted testicle that cuts off blood supply).
common_complications: None

name: Cystoscopy with retrograde pyelography (x-ray evaluation of urinary system)
description: Along with cystoscopy the provider injects contrast into one or both ureters. These are the tubes that connect the bladder to the kidneys. An x-ray is done enabling a view of the ureters and kidneys. The procedure can detect kidney stones, strictures, cysts, and tumors.
common_complications: Perforation of the bladder, injury of the ureter, or allergic reaction to the contrast dye. Infection after the procedure.

name: Ureteroscopy (camera examination of tubes between kidney and bladder)
description: A small lighted tube is inserted through the urethra and bladder into the ureter (the tube connecting the bladder and kidneys). The scope is equipped with an instrument that can open blockages and/or help remove kidney stones stuck in the ureter.
common_complications: Infection. Rarely bladder or ureter perforation. Patients can infrequently have a bad reaction to anesthesia.

name: Transrectal ultrasound with prostate biopsy (ultrasound guided prostate tissue sample)
description: A diagnostic imaging procedure to guide prostate biopsy. An ultrasound (sonogram) consists of high frequency sound waves. An ultrasound device is inserted into the rectum to view the prostate, measure the prostate size and identify areas of concern. The device has an attachment that can take needle biopsies. The procedure is done to diagnose cancer.
common_complications: The main risks of the procedure include infection and bleeding from the rectum or bladder. There may be blood in the semen with ejaculation for 2-3 weeks following the procedure.

name: GreenLight PVPTM (Photo-selective Vaporization of the Prostate, laser)
description: GreenLight PVPTM (Photo-selective Vaporization of the Prostate) is a laser treatment for benign prostatic hyperplasia to reduce prostate size. During the procedure a thin fiber is inserted into the urethra through a cystoscope and green laser energy is applied to the prostate. The reduction in the size of the prostate allows better urinary flow.
common_complications: Complications include: bleeding from the bladder, infection, and painful urination. Longer term complications include retrograde ejaculation, incontinence, and erectile dysfunction (impotence).

name: Prostate needle biopsy (needle tissue sample of prostate)
description: A fine needle is inserted into the prostate to obtain tissue for analysis. The procedure is done to diagnose prostate cancer.
common_complications: Infection, bleeding at the biopsy site. There may be blood in the semen with ejaculation for 2-3 weeks following the procedure.

name: Cystometrogram (CMG, bladder function test)
description: A cystometrogram measures the bladder's ability to store, contract, and expel urine. A catheter is inserted into a patient's bladder and fluid is inserted to fill the bladder. Pressure measurements are taken after the catheter is removed and the person tries to urinate. The test is generally done when people have problems with urinary retention and/or incontinence.
common_complications: Complications include: painful urination after the procedure, infection, and noticeable blood in the urine.

name: Prostate specific antigen (PSA, prostate cancer screening blood test)
description: Prostate-specific antigen (PSA) is a protein produced by cells of the prostate gland. The level is measured with a blood test. The amount of PSA increases as the prostate enlarges with age. PSA levels also increase from prostate infections, with prostate cancer, and with trauma to the prostate. The levels are followed over time and are used by the provider to map out a treatment plan. Not all patients with an elevated PSA require further evaluation and/or treatment. Discussions with the treating doctor and patient will determine the best options.
common_complications: None

name: Carpal tunnel surgery  (open release surgery, wrist nerve)
description: Open release surgery is performed to treat carpal tunnel syndrome. A 2-inch incision is made over the wrist.The carpal tunnel ligament is cut to make more room in the carpal tunnel and take pressure off the median nerve. The procedure is generally done as an outpatient under local anesthesia.
common_complications: Complications include: infection, nerve injury, and/or wrist stiffness. Pain may persist despite surgery.

name: Urinalysis (UA, microscopic examination of urine)
description: A urinalysis is a simple and common test to help detect urinary tract infections, and other bladder and kidney problems. The urine is analyzed for the presence of protein, blood, glucose and other substances. The urine is also examined under microscope for white blood cells, red blood cells and bacteria. The presence of white blood cells indicates an infection and red blood cells are seen in traumatic injuries, kidney stones and other diseases.
common_complications: None

name: Blood test for heart damage (troponin test)
description: Troponin is a protein that is released into the blood stream when heart muscle is damaged.  A blood test for troponin and an electrocardiogram (ECG) are the most commonly used tests to diagnose a heart attack.
common_complications: None

name: Angiogram, arm (x-ray of upper extremity blood vessels)
description: An angiogram is a procedure that uses x-ray imaging to see the inside of the arteries. An intravenous dye is injected into the artery of the arm and x-rays are taken to view the blood vessel. The test is done to detect blockages of the artery, tears of the artery, and abnormal enlargements of the artery called aneurysms.
common_complications: The artery can be damaged when the needle is inserted into the vessel. Patients can have an allergic reaction to the intravenous dye and rarely the reaction can be life threatening. The dye can also injure the kidneys. Patients with pre-existing kidney disease and diabetes are more likely to develop kidney damage from the dye.

name: Endoscopic carpal tunnel surgery (minimally invasive wrist surgery)
description: Traditional carpal tunnel surgery requires a 2 inch incision to reach the carpal ligament. With the endoscopic technique one or two 1/2 inch incisions are made. A small camera is inserted into the incision to visualize and cut the carpal ligament causing the constriction and pressure on the median nerve. The procedure is generally done as an outpatient under local anesthesia.
common_complications: Complications include: infection, nerve injury, wrist stiffness, and/or wrist weakness. Pain may persist despite surgery.

name: Cervical discectomy (neck disc surgery)
description: Cervical discectomy with fusion involves relieving the pressure on the nerves or spinal cord by removing the offending disc. A bone graft is placed between the bones above and below where the disc was removed, which fuses the two bones together. The surgeon reaches the disc by making an incision in the front of the neck (anterior) and the operation is often called an anterior cervical discectomy. Hardware may be inserted to help stabilize the bones and speed healing after surgery.
common_complications: Complications include: hoarseness, swallowing problems, degeneration of the adjacent vertebrae, fractures of the hardware installed, migration of the bone graft requiring a second surgery, nerve damage and chronic pain. All surgery comes with the risk of infection and blood clots. Patients can infrequently have bad reactions to the general anesthesia.

name: Decompression laminectomy (removal of back of spinal bones)
description: Decompression laminectomy is the removal of the entire bony lamina, a portion of the enlarged facet joints, and the thickened ligaments overlying the spinal cord and nerves. The lamina are two broad plates, extending posteriorly from the pedicles, fusing together to complete the roof of the vertebral arch. Reasons for this surgery include spinal stenosis, degenerative disk disease, herniated disc, and sciatica.
common_complications: Complications include: Nerve damage, persistent pain. All surgery comes with the risk of infection and blood clots. Patients can infrequently have bad reactions to anesthesia.

name: Foraminotomy (spinal nerve decompression)
description: Foraminotomy is a surgical procedure done to relieve pressure on a nerve as it exits the spinal canal. The openings to allow nerves to exit the spine are called neural foramina. Most often the pressure is cause by bone spurs or ligaments. The most common reason for the surgery is sciatica or other persistent nerve pain caused by a narrowed neural foramen.
common_complications: Complications include: nerve damage or persistent pain. All surgery comes with the risk of infection and blood clots. Patients can infrequently have bad reactions to anesthesia.

name: Lumbar fusion (surgical fusion of lower spine vertebrae)
description: A lumbar fusion is the locking together (fusing) of multiple spinal vertebrae of the back to help relieve the pressure placed on the nerves from movement of the spine. The surgeon removes the disc material between the vertebrae and replaces it with a bone graft. Sometimes metal hardware is placed to bridge the vertebrae as well. The bone graft can be taken from the patient's hip (autograft bone) during the spine fusion surgery, harvested from cadaver bone (allograft bone) or manufactured (synthetic bone graft substitute). Reasons for the surgery include pain and numbness caused by a herniated disc, spinal stenosis, and spondylolisthesis.
common_complications: Complications include: vertebrae failing to fuse, hardware fracture, bone graft migration, nerve damage or persistent pain. All surgery comes with the risk of infection and blood clots. Patients can infrequently have bad reactions to anesthesia.

name: Anterior cervical fusion (neck fusion)
description: An anterior cervical fusion is the locking together (fusing) of multiple spinal vertebrae of the neck to help relieve the pressure placed on the nerves from movement of the spine caused by spinal stenosis, herniated disc, and bone spurs. The surgeon approaches the spine from the front of the neck (anterior), removes the disc material between the vertebrae, and replaces it with a bone graft. The bone graft allows the vertebrae to fuse together. The bone graft can be taken from the patient's hip (autograft bone) during the spine fusion surgery, harvested from cadaver bone (allograft bone) or manufactured (synthetic bone graft substitute). Hardware may be used to help bridge the vertebrae together.
common_complications: Complications include: hoarseness, swallowing problems, degeneration of the adjacent vertebrae, failure of the hardware installed, migration of the bone graft, nerve damage and chronic pain. All surgery comes with the risk of infection and blood clots. Patients can infrequently have bad reactions to anesthesia.

name: Posterolateral gutter fusion (surgical fusion of spinal bones)
description: A posterolateral gutter fusion is a type of lumbar fusion. A lumbar fusion is the locking together (fusing) of multiple spinal vertebrae of the back to help relieve the pressure placed on the nerves from movement of the spine. The surgeon approaches the spine from the posterior lateral area of the back. Disc material between the vertebrae is removed, and replaced it with a bone graft.  Metal hardware may be used to help bridge the vertebrae together. The bone graft can be taken from the patient's hip (autograft bone) during the spine fusion surgery, harvested from cadaver bone (allograft bone) or manufactured (synthetic bone graft substitute). Reasons for the surgery include pain and numbness caused by a herniated disc, spinal stenosis, and spondylolisthesis.
common_complications: Complications include: vertebrae failing to fuse, hardware fracture, bone graft migration, nerve damage or persistent pain. All surgery comes with the risk of infection and blood clots. Patients can infrequently have bad reactions to anesthesia.

name: Posterior lumbar interbody fusion (PLIF, fusion of lower spinal bones)
description: A type of lumbar fusion procedure. A lumbar fusion is the locking together (fusing) of multiple spinal vertebrae of the back to help relieve the pressure placed on the nerves from movement of the spine. The procedure is done from the back and includes removing the disc between two vertebrae and inserting a bone graft into the space created between the two vertebral bodies. The bone graft can be taken from the patient's hip (autograft bone) during the spine fusion surgery, harvested from cadaver bone (allograft bone) or manufactured (synthetic bone graft substitute). Reasons for the surgery include pain and numbness caused by a herniated disc, spinal stenosis, and spondylolisthesis.
common_complications: Complications include: vertebrae failing to fuse, hardware fracture, bone graft migration, nerve damage or persistent pain. All surgery comes with the risk of infection and blood clots. Patients can infrequently have bad reactions to anesthesia.

name: Anterior lumbar interbody fusion (ALIF, fusion of back bones)
description: A type of lumbar fusion procedure. The surgery is done by approaching the spine from the front though the abdomen. The disc material between two vertebrae is removed and bone material is inserted to produce the fusion. Sometimes a posterior fusion is performed as well. Reasons for the surgery include pain and numbness caused by a herniated disc, spinal stenosis, and spondylolisthesis.
common_complications: Complications include: vertebrae failing to fuse, hardware failure, bone graft migration, nerve damage or persistent pain. All surgery comes with the risk of infection and blood clots. Patients can infrequently have bad reactions to anesthesia.

name: Anterior posterior spinal fusion (fusion of front, back of spine)
description: A type of lumbar fusion. The surgeon performs both anterior and posterior fusion to achieve maximum spine stability. A lumbar fusion is the locking together (fusing) of multiple spinal vertebrae of the back to help relieve the pressure placed on the nerves from movement of the spine. Reasons for the surgery include pain and numbness caused by a herniated disc, spinal stenosis, and spondylolisthesis. Hardware is often used to stabilize the spine. This type of surgery is usually done when the spine is particularly unstable.
common_complications: Complications include: vertebrae failing to fuse, hardware failure, bone graft migration, nerve damage or persistent pain. All surgery comes with the risk of infection and blood clots. Patients can infrequently have bad reactions to anesthesia.

name: Disc replacement (spinal disc replacement)
description: Replacing the damaged disc between the vertebrae with an artificial disc is an alternative to a spinal fusion for chronic back and neck pain secondary to degenerative disc disease and a herniated disc.
common_complications: Complications include: chronic pain form nerve damage; a necessary repeat surgical procedure from failure of the artificial disc. All surgery comes with the risk of infection and blood clots. Patients can infrequently have bad reactions to anesthesia.

name: Deep Brain Stimulation (DBS, electrode implantation in brain)
description: Deep brain stimulation (DBS) is a neurosurgical treatment which involves the implantation of a brain pacemaker that stimulates the brain with mild electrical signals. The procedure is done to treat Parkinson's disease not responding to drug therapy. It has also been used to treat chronic pain, tremor and dystonia.
common_complications: Complications include changes in personality and behavior such as: apathy, hallucinations, compulsive gambling, hypersexuality, cognitive dysfunction, and depression. Risks from anesthesia depend on the type use for the procedure.

name: Anterior cervical corpectomy (removal of neck bone, disc)
description: The spine is approached from the anterior (front) part of the neck. The surgeon removes a vertebra and disc material that is causing pressure on the spinal cord (spinal stenosis). The surgeon then proceeds with a neck fusion using hardware to stabilize the spine.
common_complications: Complications include: hoarseness, swallowing problems, degeneration of the adjacent vertebrae, failure of the hardware installed, migration of the bone graft, nerve damage and chronic pain. All surgery comes with the risk of infection and blood clots. Patients can infrequently have bad reactions to the general anesthesia.

name: Microdiscectomy (removal of small portion of disk, bone in spine)
description: A small portion of the bone and/or disc material that is impinging on the nerve is removed. The procedure is done to relieve the pain of a herniated disc. The surgery is more effective in relieving leg pain than back pain and is much less invasive than a total removal of the disc and fusion.
common_complications: Complications include chronic pain and failure of the procedure requiring a repeat procedure. All surgery comes with the risk of infection and blood clots. Patients can infrequently have bad reactions to anesthesia.

name: Percutaneous discectomy (minimally invasive removal of spinal disk)
description: Small instruments are inserted through the skin into the disc between the vertebrae. The disc material is removed by cutting it out or using a laser to remove the material. X-rays are used to guide the instrument. The procedure is done to relieve the pain of a herniated disc. It can usually be performed using local anesthesia.
common_complications: Complications include infection, persistent pain and failure of the procedure requiring a repeat procedure.

name: Percutaneous endoscopic laser discectomy (minimally invasive laser removal of spinal disk)
description: Percutaneous endoscopic laser discectomy is a type of percutaneous discectomy where the surgeon uses a laser to remove the disc material. A small laser is inserted through the skin guided by x-rays. The procedure is done to relieve the pain of a herniated disc. It can usually be performed using local anesthesia.
common_complications: Complications include infection, persistent pain and failure of the procedure requiring a repeat procedure.

name: Percutaneous pedicle screws (minimally invasive spinal stabilization)
description: Pedicle screws are used to stabilize the spine and allow the vertebrae to fuse. Pedicle screws are connected with rods. These screws are usually placed through an open incision. In the percutaneous route the screws are placed through a small skin incision, often referred to as a minimally invasive technique.
common_complications: Complications include: vertebrae failing to fuse, hardware fracture, nerve damage and/or persistent pain. All surgery comes with the risk of infection and blood clots. Patients can infrequently have bad reactions to anesthesia.

name: Transforaminal lumbar interbody fusion (TLIF, lower back spinal fusion)
description: Transforaminal lumbar interbody fusion (TLIF) is a type of lumbar fusion. A lumbar fusion is the locking together (fusing) of multiple spinal vertebrae of the back to help relieve the pressure placed on the nerves from movement of the spine. The bone graft can be taken from the patient's hip (autograft bone) during the spine fusion surgery, harvested from cadaver bone (allograft bone) or manufactured (synthetic bone graft substitute). The front portion of the spine is stabilized with a bone graft and interbody spacer. The rear column is secured in place with pedicle screws, rods, and bone graft.
common_complications: Complications include: vertebrae failing to fuse, hardware fracture, bone graft migration, nerve damage and/or persistent pain. All surgery comes with the risk of infection and blood clots. Patients can infrequently have bad reactions to anesthesia.

name: Vertebroplasty (minimally invasive treatment of spine fracture)
description: Vertebroplasty is a procedure used to treat compression fractures of the thoracic and lumbar spine. Using x-ray guidance a needle is inserted into the compressed vertebra and acrylic cement is inserted. When the cement dries the bone regains stability and strength.
common_complications: Complications include: leaking of acrylic cement outside of the vertebral body, infection, bleeding, numbness, and tingling. The patient may continue to have back pain following the procedure.

name: Lumbar facet rhizotomy (deadening of spinal nerves with heat)
description: A procedure that is used to treat lower back pain being caused by an irritated nerve near a facet joint of the lower back. A needle is inserted into the back near the nerve causing the pain. A small wire is passed through the needle and a radio frequency current is used to deaden the nerve.
common_complications: Complications include bleeding, infection, and nerve damage. Nerve damage can result in increased pain, numbness, and/or leg weakness.

name: Lumbar facet joint injection (low back joint injection for pain)
description: A procedure that is used to treat lower back pain being caused by an irritated nerve near a facet joint of the lower back. A needle is inserted near the irritated nerve causing the pain. A local anesthetic and a corticosteroid are injected into the area. The anesthetic usually gives some immediate relief and the corticosteroid may diminish pain for months. If the pain returns a more permanent procedure such as a lumbar facet rhizotomy is considered.
common_complications: Complications include bleeding, infection, allergic reaction, and nerve damage. Nerve damage can result in increased pain, numbness and/or leg weakness.

name: Epidural steroid injection (ESI, injection into space around spinal cord)
description: An epidural steroid injection is performed to help relieve back pain or leg pain caused by spinal stenosis, degenerative disc disease, sciatica, spondylolysis, or a herniated disc. A needle is inserted into the sac surrounding the spinal cord and nerves but does not enter the area containing the spinal cord. A local anesthetic and a corticosteroid are injected into this area. The anesthetic usually gives some immediate relief and the corticosteroid may diminish pain for several weeks or more.
common_complications: Complications include bleeding, infection, allergic reaction, and nerve damage. Nerve damage can result in increased pain, numbness and/or leg weakness.

name: Arthrography (x-ray of joint)
description: Arthrography is performed to outline the joints and ligaments. A dye is inserted into the joint and x-rays are taken to identify any injuries.
common_complications: Infection, bleeding, or allergic reaction to the dye.

name: Bone scintigraphy (bone scan)
description: Bone scintigraphy, also called a bone scan, is a diagnostic test to create images of bones for evaluation. Radioactive material is injected into a blood vessel and collects in the bones. It is then detected by a scanner. A bone scan detects increased metabolic activity and can be used to diagnose bone infections, fractures or cancer.
common_complications: Rarely an allergic reaction to the injected radioactive material can occur.

name: Electromyogram (EMG, recording of muscle electricity)
description: An electromyogram (EMG), also called electromyography, is a test that measures the electrical activity of the muscle at rest and with contractions. The impulses are measured by inserting needle electrodes into the muscle. The EMG graphs this electrical activity. An EMG is used to help diagnose diseases, such as muscular dystrophy, myositis (inflammation of the muscles), peripheral nerve damage, amyotrophic lateral sclerosis, myasthenia gravis, carpal tunnel syndrome, and a pinched nerve from a herniated disc.
common_complications: Complications are rare. The nerve or muscle can be irritated from insertion of the electrodes.

name: Video fluoroscopy (x-rays that capture motion of a body part)
description: Video fluoroscopy uses a video to capture and store a rapid series of x-ray pictures as a person performs a bodily function, such as swallowing. The video enables the doctor to watch the function of the body in real time motion. It is used most often to detect swallowing problems.
common_complications: Complications of a single video swallow are rare.

name: Carpal tunnel release (mini open technique, wrist nerve)
description: In the mini open carpal tunnel release the surgeon makes a 1 inch incision over the carpal tunnel ligament to allow direct visualization during the procedure. Through this small incision the carpal tunnel ligament is cut releasing the pressure on the median nerve. The procedure is done to help relieve numbness, pain and weakness in the hand. This technique tends to cause less pain and it may minimize scarring and stiffness afterward.
common_complications: Complications include: pain, increased numbness and tingling, infection, scarring, stiffness and diminished wrist strength.

name: Needle aponeurotomy (minimally invasive treatment of bent fingers)
description: Needle aponeurotomy is a procedure to reduce the contraction caused by the diseased palmar fascia in Dupuytren's contracture. Very small puncture wounds are made in the hand and the tip of a needle is used to divide the contracted palmar fascia.
common_complications: Complications include infection from the needle insertion and/or nerve damage.

name: Arthroplasty (joint surgery)
description: Arthroplasty is the general term for surgery to improve joint function. The most common type is to replace the affected joint with an artificial joint. Other techniques involve removing bone and scar tissue around the joint to increase movement.
common_complications: Complications include bleeding, infection, blood clots and reactions to anesthesia. Other complications are dependent on the joint being repaired.

name: Joint fusion (arthrodesis)
description: Joint fusion is surgery that decreases the movement of the joint. It can be done on any joint in the body and is usually performed to improve stability and decrease pain.
common_complications: Complications include bleeding, infection, blood clots and reactions to anesthesia. Other complications are dependent on the joint being fused.

name: Knee arthroplasty (knee replacement)
description: A surgical procedure to replace the knee with an artificial joint. The damaged cartilage and bone of the knee joint (tibia, femur, and patella) are replaced with a combination of metal and plastic components. The most common reasons for knee replacement are arthritis and other conditions which deteriorate the cartilage and bone of the joint.
common_complications: Knee stiffness, blood loss and nerve injury are risks. The surgery can result in post-operative pain, infection or blood clots of the legs (deep vein thrombosis) or lungs (pulmonary embolus). Patients can infrequently have bad reactions to the general anesthesia including allergic reactions and very rarely a heart attack or stroke.

name: Hip arthroplasty (hip replacement)
description: A surgical procedure to replace the hip with an artificial joint. The cup shaped hip socket and the ball of the thigh bone are replaced with metal and plastic components.  The most common reasons for hip replacement are arthritis and other conditions which deteriorate the cartilage and bone of the joint.
common_complications: Joint dislocation, bone fracture, hardware fracture, loosening of the joint, and change in leg length are all risks. The surgery can result in post-operative pain, infection or blood clots of the legs (deep vein thrombosis) or lungs (pulmonary embolus). Patients can infrequently have bad reactions to the general anesthesia including allergic reactions and very rarely a heart attack or stroke.

name: Arthroscopic surgery (joint surgery using camera)
description: Arthroscopic surgery involves the insertion of a tube with a camera into the joint and examination of the inside of the joint. Many times the problem can be identified and repaired at the same time. Many joints can be repaired with this procedure but the knee is the most common.
common_complications: Complications include infection, injury to the joint, ligaments, cartilage, nerves or blood vessels. Patients can infrequently have bad reactions to anesthesia.

name: Rotator cuff repair (shoulder muscle repair)
description: The rotator cuff is part of the shoulder joint and is made up of 4 muscles and tendons. Surgery is done primarily to repair the tendons, and remove bone spurs. The procedure can be performed through a larger incision (open technique) or through a tube with a camera requiring only a small incision (arthroscopic technique).
common_complications: Complications include infection, injury to the joint, ligaments, cartilage, nerves or blood vessels. Patients can infrequently have bad reactions to anesthesia. Stiffness of the shoulder, failure of the surgery to relieve symptoms, failure of the repair to heal and weakness of the shoulder may occur.

name: Laparoscopic banding (weight loss surgery)
description: A type of weight loss surgery. The surgeon inserts a band around the upper part of the stomach creating a small pouch. This procedure makes the stomach smaller causing patients to feel full after eating small amounts of food. The procedure has been demonstrated to help patients lose weight and decrease the risk of type 2 diabetes. Some patients that already have diabetes have normal sugar levels after the surgery. There are different types of bands. Some are adjustable by adding or removing fluid from the band through a valve under the skin.
common_complications: Complications include: injury to the stomach, frequent nausea and vomiting, damage to the surrounding intestines, inflammation of the stomach (gastritis), heartburn, stomach ulcers, and malnutrition. Scarring inside the abdomen can result in intestinal obstruction. All surgery comes with the risk of infection and blood clots. Patients can infrequently have bad reactions to anesthesia.

name: Disk removal (spinal disk removal)
description: A surgical procedure to remove part of a herniated disk in the spine. This can relieve some of the pressure on a nerve causing pain in the neck, back or leg.
common_complications: Spinal fluid leak and nerve injury. A recurrent herniated disc can occur. Any surgery can result in pain, infection or blood clots of the legs (deep vein thrombosis) or lungs (pulmonary embolus). Patients can infrequently have bad reactions to anesthesia.

name: Tenotomy (cutting of a tendon)
description: Tenotomy is the cutting of a tendon. The procedure is done to lengthen a muscle that has been shortened. It is most commonly done to treat a club foot, a contracted bicep or a shortened Achilles tendon.
common_complications: Complications include injury to the joint, ligaments, cartilage, nerves or blood vessels. All surgery comes with the risk of infection and blood clots. Patients can infrequently have bad reactions to anesthesia.

name: Ganglion cyst removal
description: Ganglion cyst removal, or ganglionectomy, is the removal of a fluid filled sac found over the wrist, finger or bottom of the foot. The procedure consists of draining the fluid with a needle, followed by removal of the cyst surgically.
common_complications: Complications include injury to the joint, ligaments, cartilage, nerves or blood vessels. All surgery comes with the risk of infection.

name: Bone grafting (bone replacement)
description: Bone grafting is a procedure that places bone in an area to stimulate bone growth. The procedure is commonly performed when a fracture doesn't heal correctly, to strengthen a bone, or to fuse a joint. If the bone comes from another person it is called an allograft. The most common allograft donors are from a person who has died (cadaver donor). If the bone graft is taken from the patient it is called an autograft. The most common donor sites for an autograft are the pelvis and lower leg.
common_complications: Failure of the graft to stimulate bone growth.  All surgery comes with the risk of infection.

name: Bankart procedure (shoulder stabilization surgery)
description: A Bankart procedure, also known as a Broca-Perthes-Bankart procedure, is performed to stabilize a shoulder that is frequently coming out of joint (dislocating). The surgery can be performed through a skin incision (open procedure) or through an arthroscope.
common_complications: Complications include infection, injury to the joint, ligaments, cartilage, nerves or blood vessels. Patients can infrequently have bad reactions to anesthesia. Stiffness of the shoulder, failure of the surgery to relieve symptoms, and/or failure of the repair to stop recurrent dislocations may occur.

name: Shoulder joint replacement
description: Shoulder joint replacement surgery involves replacing the joint with a prosthesis. Reasons for the procedure include chronic pain and loss of movement from joint damage. The most common causes of joint damage include: osteoarthritis, rheumatoid arthritis, trauma including fractures, rotator cuff injuries, avascular necrosis, and failed previous shoulder surgeries. Most patients can perform simple tasks 2 weeks after surgery.
common_complications: Complications include infection, injury to the joint, ligaments, cartilage, nerves or blood vessels. Patients can infrequently have bad reactions to the general anesthesia. The surgery may not relieve the stiffness or chronic pain of the shoulder.  Additional complications may include:  dislocation of the artificial joint, loosening of the artificial joint over time, or allergic reaction to the artificial joint.

name: Hip osteotomy (hip joint reshaping)
description: A surgical procedure in which the bones of the hip joint are cut, reoriented, and fixed in a new position. The procedure is performed to orient the weight bearing of the femur in line with areas of healthy cartilage. Typically a metal plate or pin is placed to keep the femur in its new orientation. Two common types of hip osteotomy are varus rotational osteotomy and pelvic osteotomy.
common_complications: Complications include injury to the joint, ligaments, cartilage, nerves or blood vessels. All surgery comes with the risk of infection and blood clots. Patients can infrequently have bad reactions to the general anesthesia. The surgery may not relieve the stiffness or chronic pain of the hip.

name: Hip revision surgery (artificial hip joint repair)
description: Hip revision surgery (total hip arthroplasty) is a procedure that repairs a previous hip replacement surgery. The surgeon removes the artificial hip joint (prosthesis) and replaces it with a new artificial joint. Sometimes a bone graft will be performed as well. The most common reasons for an artificial joint to stop functioning are normal wear and tear and infection.
common_complications: Complications include injury to the joint, ligaments, cartilage, nerves or blood vessels. All surgery comes with the risk of infection and blood clots. Patients can infrequently have bad reactions to the general anesthesia including allergic reactions and very rarely a heart attack or stroke. The surgery may not relieve the stiffness or chronic pain of the hip. Additional complications may include:  dislocation of the artificial joint, loosening of the artificial joint over time, or allergic reaction to the artificial joint.

name: Knee revision surgery (artificial knee joint repair)
description: Knee revision surgery (total knee arthroplasty) is a procedure that repairs a previous knee replacement surgery. The surgeon removes the artificial knee joint (prosthesis) and replaces it with a new artificial joint. Sometimes a bone graft will be performed as well. The most common reasons for an artificial joint to stop functioning are normal wear and tear and infection.
common_complications: Complications include injury to the joint, ligaments, cartilage, nerves or blood vessels. All surgery comes with the risk of infection and blood clots. Patients can infrequently have bad reactions to the general anesthesia including allergic reactions and very rarely a heart attack or stroke. The surgery may not relieve the stiffness or chronic pain of the knee. Additional complications may include:  dislocation of the artificial joint, loosening of the artificial joint over time, or allergic reaction to the artificial joint.

name: Finger reattachment
description: Surgery performed to reattach an amputated finger. The amputated finger should be wrapped in clean moist dressing (preferably sterile gauze) and placed in a plastic bag and brought to the hospital or doctor as quickly as possible.
common_complications: Infection, a reaction to anesthesia and/or failure of reattachment.

name: Kneecap removal (patellectomy)
description: The removal of the kneecap also called patellectomy. The patella may be removed because of persistent or very frequent patella dislocations, chronic pain or after severe fractures.
common_complications: Complications include injury to the joint, ligaments, cartilage, nerves or blood vessels.  All surgery comes with the risk of infection and blood clots. Patients can infrequently have bad reactions to anesthesia. The surgery may result in knee stiffness and may not improve chronic knee pain.

name: Shoulder resection arthroplasty (shoulder joint surgical repair)
description: Surgery that removes the end of the collar bone (clavicle) and reconstructs the acromio clavicular (AC) joint. Injury or arthritis can damage the AC joint leading to decreased shoulder motion and pain. This procedure helps to relieve these symptoms.
common_complications: Complications include injury to the joint, ligaments, cartilage, nerves or blood vessels. All surgery comes with the risk of infection and blood clots. Patients can infrequently have bad reactions to the general anesthesia. The surgery may not relieve the stiffness or chronic pain of the shoulder.

name: Leg lengthening and shortening
description: A surgical procedure that is performed to correct leg length differences.  Surgery consists of lengthening a leg, shortening a leg or preventing a leg from continued growth. The type of surgery depends on the amount of length difference between the two legs and the age of the patient. Surgery is usually performed early in life.
common_complications: Complications include injury to the joint, ligaments, cartilage, nerves or blood vessels. All surgery comes with the risk of infection and blood clots. Patients can infrequently have bad reactions to anesthesia. The surgery may not produce the desired result.

name: Webbed finger or toe repair
description: Surgery performed to repair a birth defect consisting of fusion of the fingers or toes, also called syndactyly. The tissue between the fused fingers or toes usually consists of just skin. Rarely there can also be bone, nerves, muscle and/or blood vessels. The most commonly affected digits are the long and ring fingers, and the second and third toes. Surgical repair is usually performed between the ages 6 and 24 months. Rarely webbing of the fingers or toes occurs from severe burn injuries.
common_complications: Complications are uncommon, but may include infection or reaction to the anesthesia. The surgery may not produce the desired result.

name: Ultraviolet light B (UVB, skin disease light treatment)
description: UVB is ultraviolet light B and is a form of phototherapy used to treat psoriasis. There is a narrow and wide band type of UVB. Studies have revealed the narrow band to be more effective. The UVB penetrates the skin and slows down the growth of skin cells that cause psoriasis. The treatments are done on a regular basis and can be given in the office or in the home.
common_complications: Initially there may be nausea, itching, and skin redness. These side effects usually diminish with further treatments.

name: PUVA treatment (UVA and psoralen, light therapy)
description: PUVA is UVA (ultraviolet light A) combined with the medication psoralen to treat psoriasis. Psoralen can be applied topically or taken as a pill. UVA alone is not effective. PUVA works the best on guttate psoriasis, stable plaque psoriasis, and psoriasis involving the soles of the feet and palms of the hands.
common_complications: Initially there may be nausea, itching, and skin redness. These side effects usually diminish with further treatments.

name: Mohs micrographic surgery (skin cancer removal surgery)
description: An office based surgery that removes skin cancer. It is most effective for basal cell carcinomas but is also used for squamous cell cancers and certain types of melanomas. The doctor removes very thin layers of cells and each layer is immediately viewed under a microscope to ensure all the cancer is removed while minimizing the amount of damage done to healthy tissue. The procedure is recommended for cancers where a scar would be very visible, in cancers with hard to determine borders, and for large aggressive cancers.
common_complications: Bleeding, pain and infection are the most common side effects.

name: Blue light acne treatment (light therapy)
description: A high intensity narrow band of blue light is applied to areas of acne to kill the bacteria thought to cause acne, Propionibacterium acnes (P. acnes). Since these bacteria grow rapidly multiple treatments are needed.
common_complications: Swelling, redness, stinging and burning following treatment.

name: Microcurrent facial (non-invasive electrical face lift)
description: A non-surgical technique that is thought to improve the appearance of the skin. Gentle electric currents are used to stimulate the skin cells to produce chemicals that improve the appearance of the skin. The procedure is painless and does not require any anesthesia.
common_complications: Mild irritation of the skin.

name: Thermage (noninvasive cosmetic skin procedure)
description: A procedure that uses radio waves to tighten and firm the skin. Can be used to remove wrinkles and unwanted contours. The radio waves heat up a protein in the skin called collagen causing it to contract. The contraction of the collagen causes the skin to tighten and remove wrinkles. Initially the procedure was only performed on the face but now can be used in other areas of the body. The procedure takes about an hour in the doctor's office. Thermage is best recommended for wrinkles that are less than 2mm in depth. The results last 6-24 months.
common_complications: Swelling, redness, blisters, peeling, bumps and/or dimpling. Side effects are rare and generally resolve in a short period of time.

name: Endoluminal gastroplication (ELGP, minimally invasive GERD treatment)
description: A treatment for chronic gastroesophageal reflux disease (GERD). The doctor performs an endoscopy (a flexible tube with a cameras inserted through the mouth into the esophagus). Through the endoscope pieces of esophagus are sutured into a pleat (plicated) just below the lower esophageal sphincter. These pleats reduce the acidic stomach contents from entering the esophagus and reduce the symptoms of GERD. The procedure is performed as an outpatient procedure.
common_complications: Complications include injury to the esophagus or throat, bleeding of the esophagus, pain, and failure of the procedure to reduce the GERD symptoms. Rarely perforation of the esophagus can lead to a life threatening problem. The anesthesia runs the risk of allergic reactions.

name: Esophageal pH test (measurement of esophageal acid)
description: The test measures the acidity (pH) in the esophagus. A low pH means stomach acid is refluxing back up into the esophagus. This helps diagnose gastroesophageal reflux disease (GERD). A tube is inserted through the nose into the esophagus just above the lower esophageal sphincter. The pH is monitored for a 12-24 hour period.
common_complications: Complications are rare. Minor discomfort can occur when the tube is inserted through the nose.

name: Flexible sigmoidoscopy (camera examination of colon)
description: A flexible tube with a camera is inserted into the rectum. The doctor examines the inside of the rectum and the last part of the colon called the sigmoid colon. Reasons for the procedure include screening for colorectal cancer and to help diagnose infections and inflammatory bowel disease, such as Crohn's disease or ulcerative colitis.
common_complications: Discomfort and bloating. Injury to the rectum or lower colon. Colonic perforation can rarely occur.

name: Hydrogen breath test (test for bacterial overgrowth)
description: A test used to detect lactose intolerance or excessive bacteria growth in the intestine. After fasting for 12 hours the patient breathes into a balloon to measure the amount of hydrogen. The patient then drinks a sweet solution and similar breath samples are taken every 15-120 minutes to measure the amount of hydrogen.
common_complications: Complications are very rare.

name: Liver biopsy (liver tissue removal)
description: A sample of the liver is taken to examine under the microscope. A liver biopsy is usually performed in one of two ways. A percutaneous liver biopsy involves inserting a needle through the skin of the abdomen into the liver and obtaining a small piece of liver tissue. A transjugular liver biopsy involves putting a catheter into the jugular vein and advancing it into the liver. Once inside the liver, a special biopsy tool is inserted through the catheter to obtain a small piece of liver.
common_complications: Infection, bleeding, and injury to the liver or other organs.

name: Fecal fat (stool fat measurement)
description: A test that measures the amount of fat in the stool. Excessive fat is found in the feces when the patient is unable to properly digest ingested fat, a disorder called fat malabsorption.
common_complications: None

name: Lactose tolerance test (test for lactose intolerance)
description: A test that measures a patient's ability to digest lactose. Lactose is a sugar found in dairy products such as milk and cheese. The most common test is the hydrogen breath test. An older test done infrequently today is the lactose tolerance blood test.
common_complications: None

name: Rectal biopsy (tissue sample of the rectum)
description: A small piece of rectal tissue is taken to examine under the microscope to look for signs of inflammation, infection or cancer. The procedure is done through a scope inserted into the rectum.
common_complications: Pain, bleeding, infection, or perforation of the rectum.

name: Sweat test (chloride sweat test, screening test for cystic fibrosis)
description: A test that measures the amount of chloride in the sweat. It is the most commonly used non-genetic test to diagnose cystic fibrosis.
common_complications: None

name: Hysterosalpingography (x-ray of uterus and fallopian tubes)
description: A test performed to determine if the communication from the ovaries through the fallopian tubes (the tubes that connect the ovaries to the uterus) to the uterus is free of obstruction. Contrast dye is injected through the cervix into the uterus and x-rays are taken to ensure the dye reaches the ovaries. The most common reason to perform this test is to help determine the cause of infertility.
common_complications: Allergic reaction to the contrast, uterine infection, fallopian tube infection, pain and a hole in the uterus (perforation).

name: Intrauterine insemination (IUI, infertility treatment)
description: A flexible tube is inserted into the uterus and washed sperm are inserted into the uterus. The procedure is done just after the ovary has released an egg (ovulation) in an attempt to create a pregnancy.
common_complications: Pain, cramping, infection and multiple pregnancies. The patient may not become pregnant.

name: In vitro fertilization (IVF, infertility treatment)
description: A method to fertilize eggs outside the body. A woman's egg and a man's sperm are joined in a laboratory dish. The embryo (combined egg and sperm) are then implanted into the uterus. This process is called an embryo transfer. The steps of the procedure include: stimulating the ovaries to make eggs (ovulation induction), collecting the eggs (follicular aspiration), combining the egg and sperm (insemination), and transferring the embryo.
common_complications: Abdominal pain, nausea, vomiting. The patient may not become pregnant.

name: Zygote intra fallopian transfer (ZIFT, infertility treatment)
description: Similar to in vitro fertilization except the combined egg and sperm (embryo) is inserted into the fallopian tube instead of the uterus as is performed with in vitro fertilization. The procedure is also referred to as tubal embryo transfer (TET). Unlike in vitro fertilization the woman must undergo laparoscopic surgery to enable the doctor to insert the embryo directly into the fallopian tube.
common_complications: Abdominal pain, nausea, vomiting. All surgery comes with the risk of infection and blood clots. Patients can infrequently have bad reactions to anesthesia including allergic reactions. The patient may not become pregnant.

name: Gamete intrafallopian transfer (GIFT, infertility treatment)
description: The woman's eggs are removed and mixed with washed sperm then immediately placed in the fallopian tubes. GIFT differs from in vitro fertilization (IVF) and Zygote Intra-Fallopian Transfer (ZIFT) since the formation of the embryo occurs within the fallopian tube instead of in the laboratory as in IVF and ZIFT. The woman must undergo laparoscopic surgery to enable the doctor to insert the embryo directly into the fallopian tube.
common_complications: Abdominal pain, nausea, vomiting. All surgery comes with the risk of infection and blood clots. Patients can infrequently have bad reactions to anesthesia including allergic reactions. The patient may not become pregnant.

name: Intra cytoplasmic sperm injection (ICSI, infertility treatment)
description: The sperm are injected directly into the eggs in the laboratory. This procedure is selected if the sperm are felt to be too weak to penetrate the egg themselves or if the numbers of sperm are too low. Once the embryos are formed they are implanted into the women using numerous techniques.
common_complications: The patient may not become pregnant.

name: Preimplantation genetic screening (identification of genetic defects)
description: The embryo made in the laboratory is tested for genetic disorders before it is transferred to the uterus.
common_complications: None

name: Gradient sperm washing, filtration and improvement (infertility treatment)
description: Special solutions are used to purify the sperm before they are combined with the egg to make embryos. The procedure produces sperm with higher likelihoods of creating viable embryos.
common_complications: None

name: Microsurgical epididymal sperm aspiration (MESA, surgical sperm removal)
description: The doctor makes an incision in the scrotal skin of the testicle and using a microscope collects sperm using a special tube called a micropipette. This produces a higher number of active sperm to be used in immediate egg combination or can be frozen for later use.
common_complications: Infection, pain or damage to the testicle.

name: Testicular sperm extraction (TESE, surgical sperm removal)
description: This technique is reserved for those men where Microsurgical Epididymal Sperm Aspiration (MESA) does not produce enough sperm. The doctor makes an incision in the scrotal skin of the testicle and a piece of testicle tissue is immediately evaluated to determine if usable sperm are present in the testicle. If mature sperm are present the procedure is completed and sperm are collected for use. Since the number of sperm is generally small the technique is usually combined with Intra cytoplasmic sperm injection (ICSI) to maximize success.
common_complications: Pain, infection or injury to the testicle or surrounding structures.

name: Testicular sperm aspiration (TESA, surgical sperm removal)
description: The doctor inserts a needle through the scrotal skin of the testicle and into the testicular tissue to extract sperm. The technique generally does not produce enough sperm for more than one cycle of in vitro fertilization.
common_complications: Pain, infection or injury to the testicle or surrounding structures.

name: Testis percutaneous biopsy (tissue sample of testicle)
description: Similar to Testicular Sperm Aspiration (TESA) this technique uses a larger needle in an attempt to obtain more usable sperm. The needle is inserted through the scrotal skin of the testicle and into the testicular tissue.
common_complications: Pain, infection or injury to the testicle or surrounding structures.

name: Testis microdissection (surgical sperm removal)
description: This procedure is reserved for men with low levels of available sperm. An incision is made in the scrotal skin of the testicle and a microscope is used to find testicular tissue that is producing usable sperm. Since this technique typically produces only small numbers of sperm these sperm must be used within 24 hours of being gathered.
common_complications: Pain, infection or injury to the testicle or surrounding structures.

name: Embryo cryopreservation (freezing and storage)
description: Embryos can be frozen immediately after fertilization for future use. If needed these embryos are thawed and then examined for viability. Not all embryos survive the freezing process but viable thawed embryos have the nearly the same success rate as unfrozen embryos. Embryos are usually frozen in the 2 to 8 cell stage.
common_complications: None

name: Micromanipulation (assisted fertilization)
description: A specialized procedure that utilizes microsurgery techniques to combine sperms and eggs. The most common procedure using this technique is intracytoplasmic sperm injection (ICSI).
common_complications: None

name: Tubal ligation (surgical female sterilization)
description: The fallopian tubes are surgically blocked to prevent pregnancy, also referred to as "tying the tubes". The fallopian tubes connect the ovaries to the uterus. After intercourse, sperm moves from the vagina, into the uterus and then into fallopian tubes to reach an egg for fertilization. The fertilized egg uses these tubes to reach the uterus for implantation in the uterine wall. The tubes can be blocked multiple different ways including cutting the tubes, clamping the tubes, burning the tubes and inserting an implant into the tubes. The procedure is usually done laparoscopically or during a C-section. Reversal of the procedure is possible but not always successful.
common_complications: The procedure can damage the bladder, intestines or ovaries. Rarely patients can still become pregnant after the procedure.  All surgery comes with the risk of infection and blood clots. Patients can infrequently have bad reactions to anesthesia.

name: Anterior cervical discectomy (neck disc surgery)
description: Cervical discectomy with fusion is most often performed to relieve pressure on the nerves or spinal cord by removing the offending disc or bony spurs. A bone graft is placed between the bones where the disc was removed. This allows the two vertebrae to fuse together. The spine is approached from the anterior (front) part of the neck. Hardware is often used to help the bones heal after surgery.
common_complications: Complications include: hoarseness, swallowing problems, degeneration of the adjacent vertebrae, failure of the installed hardware, migration of the bone graft, nerve damage and chronic pain. All surgery comes with the risk of infection and blood clots. Patients can infrequently have bad reactions to the general anesthesia.

name: C section (surgical delivery of baby)
description: A surgical procedure that removes the baby from a mother's uterus through an incision in her abdomen. A C section is also called a cesarean section and is performed when the mother cannot deliver the baby through the vagina or if the baby is in distress.
common_complications: Any major surgery can result in infection, pain, and the development of blood clots in the legs or lungs after surgery. A C-section can result in an intra-abdominal infection, intestinal obstruction, or damage to the uterus or other organs in the pelvis. Complications from anesthesia are possible but uncommon.

name: Comprehensive metabolic panel (CMP, blood test)
description: A Chem-12 is also called a Comprehensive Metabolic Panel (CMP) or a SMA-12. This test measures blood chemistries and proteins that help diagnose many conditions, including diabetes, kidney and liver diseases. The Chem-12 tests for electrolytes (sodium, potassium, carbon dioxide, and chloride), kidney tests (creatinine, blood urea nitrogen), proteins (albumin, total protein), liver tests (alkaline phosphatase, alanine amino transferase, aspartate amino transferase, bilirubin), glucose and calcium. The electrolytes become abnormal for many reasons including dehydration and adverse reactions to medications. Kidney malfunction causes the creatinine and blood urea nitrogen to increase. Problems with the liver results in elevations in the liver tests. Diabetes is diagnosed by demonstrating elevated glucose levels.
common_complications: None.

name: HDL cholesterol (high-density lipoprotein, good cholesterol)
description: HDL (high-density lipoprotein) cholesterol is considered  good cholesterol. Cholesterol is a wax-like substance in the body and is necessary for normal body function. Having too much LDL (low-density lipoprotein) or bad cholesterol can cause fatty deposits in blood vessels (atherosclerosis), which can lead to heart attacks and strokes. High levels of HDL  cholesterol are associated with a decreased risk of developing atherosclerosis.
common_complications: None

name: LDL cholesterol (low-density lipoprotein, bad cholesterol)
description: LDL (low-density lipoprotein) cholesterol is considered bad cholesterol. Cholesterol is a wax-like substance in the body and is necessary for normal body function. Too much LDL cholesterol can cause fatty deposits in blood vessels (atherosclerosis), which can lead to heart attacks and strokes.  High levels of LDL (bad cholesterol) increase the risk of developing atherosclerosis.
common_complications: None

name: Complete blood count (CBC)
description: A complete blood count (CBC) test measures the number of red blood cells (RBC), white blood cells (WBC), and platelets. The size and shape of the red blood cells, and the types of white blood cells are identified. This test is done to diagnose anemia, infections, cancer, and other blood diseases. Anemia is defined as a low hematocrit and/or low hemoglobin. Elevation of the WBC is usually associated with an infection. Platelets are needed to clot the blood and having too low a number is called thrombocytopenia.
common_complications: None

name: Computed tomography angiogram (CTA, CT image of arteries)
description: A diagnostic exam involving a CT scan and intravenous contrast that can be used to diagnose problems of the arteries of the body including aneurysms, blood clots, dissections and traumatic injuries.
common_complications: CT scans require radiation. Multiple exposures to radiation increase the risk of cancer later in life. The contrast dye used in a CTA can injure the kidneys, especially if the person has underlying kidney disease. Some patients can be allergic to the contrast resulting in a rash to life-threatening swelling and low blood pressure.

name: Coronary artery bypass graft (CABG, surgery to improve heart blood flow)
description: A surgical procedure to bypass the blockage and restore blood flow in one or more coronary (heart) arteries. For each bypassed artery, a blood vessel, usually taken from the leg or chest, is grafted into the artery above and beyond the blockage.  It can be done on one or multiple arteries. By restoring blood flow to the heart, it can prevent heart attacks.
common_complications: The major risks include heart attack, stroke, bleeding requiring surgery and death. The surgery can result in post-operative pain, infection or blood clots of the legs (deep vein thrombosis) or lungs (pulmonary embolus). Also some patients have side effects or allergic reactions to general anesthesia.

name: Sacroiliac joint injection (lower back joint injection)
description: The sacroiliac joints connect the lower back to the pelvis. There is a joint on each side of the back. Inflammation, arthritis, and/or injury of this area can cause persistent back pain. Using an x-ray for guidance a local anesthetic and steroid are injected into the area to reduce inflammation and pain.
common_complications: Pain at the site of injection. Infection or an allergic reaction to the anesthetic or injected drug can rarely occur. Symptoms may get worse despite the injection.

name: Trigger point injections (pain management treatment using muscle injections)
description: Trigger points are tight bands or "knots" of muscle that cause pain. The injections are done most often in the arms, legs, neck and/or back. A local anesthetic, often combined with a corticosteroid, is injected into the trigger point to reduce pain.
common_complications: Local pain at the injection site. Infection or an allergic reaction to the anesthetic or injected drug can rarely occur. Symptoms may get worse despite the injection.

name: Medial branch block (spinal nerve block)
description: Back pain can be caused by inflammation of the facet joints. These are the joints that connect the vertebrae (bones of the spine). The medial branch nerves are small nerves that send pain signals to the brain when the facet joints are inflamed from arthritis. Local anesthetic is injected using x-ray guidance to numb these nerves. Pain relief from the procedures implicates the facet joint as the area causing the pain and may be an indication for other procedures to produce longer lasting pain relief.
common_complications: Pain at the injection site. Rarely an infection, bleeding, or an allergic reaction from the anesthetic can occur. Symptoms may get worse despite the injection.

name: Lumbar sympathetic block (lower back injection for pain)
description: The sympathetic nerves are located on both sides along the back. At times pain is carried in the sympathetic nerves that supply the legs. A local anesthetic is injected to numb these nerves and relieve pain from conditions such as complex regional pain syndrome and post herpetic neuralgia (persistent pain from shingles).
common_complications: Pain at the site of injection. Rarely an infection, bleeding, or an allergic reaction from the anesthetic can occur. Symptoms may get worse despite the injection.

name: Radiofrequency nerve ablation (nerve block with radio waves)
description: Radio waves are used to heat one or more nerves and destroy their ability to carry pain signals to the brain. The skin over the area is numbed with a local anesthetic. Using x-ray guidance a thin needle is inserted into the area. The radio waves are directed through the needle to the nerve causing the pain. Multiple needles may need to be placed during the procedure. It is one of the treatments for facet joint arthritis.
common_complications: Pain at the site of injection. Rarely an infection, bleeding, or an allergic reaction from the anesthetic can occur. Symptoms may get worse despite the injection.

name: Stellate ganglion block (nerve block in the neck)
description: The stellate ganglion is part of the sympathetic nervous system of the neck. These sympathetic nerves supply the face, neck and arms. Pain signals from certain conditions are carried along the sympathetic nervous system. After local anesthetic of the skin, a needle is inserted in the front of the neck and anesthetic with or without a corticosteroid is injected to numb the stellate ganglion. This procedure is performed to relieve pain from conditions such as complex regional pain syndrome and post herpetic neuralgia (persistent pain from shingles).
common_complications: Pain at the site of injection. Rarely an infection, bleeding, or an allergic reaction from the anesthetic can occur. Symptoms may get worse despite the injection.

name: AC joint separation repair (acromioclavicular, shoulder joint repair)
description: Surgery to repair a torn or damaged coracoclavicular ligament. This ligament connects the acromion to the clavicle in the shoulder. Surgery is reserved for the most serious acromioclavicular joint separations (AC joint separations). The ligament is usually repaired using surrounding tissue or a graft.
common_complications: Complications include injury to the joint, ligaments, cartilage, nerves or blood vessels. All surgery comes with the risk of infection and blood clots. Patients can infrequently have bad reactions to anesthesia. Pain and/or stiffness may persist after the surgery.

name: Bunionectomy (surgical removal of bunion)
description: A bunion is also called hallux valgus. There are numerous ways to surgically fix a bunion and the procedure selected depends on the severity of the deformity and the patient. In most cases an incision is made and the excess bone is removed. The great toe is placed in proper alignment and surgical wires are used to maintain the correct position while the toe heals. The surgery can be done with local anesthesia by numbing the foot at the ankle or the patient can be given general anesthesia.
common_complications: Complications include injury to the joint, ligaments, cartilage, nerves or blood vessels. All surgery comes with the risk of infection and blood clots. Patients can infrequently have bad reactions to anesthesia. The surgery may not completely relieve pain or deformity of the foot.

name: Hammer toe repair
description: An incision is made over the affected toe and part of the tendon and joint are removed. Ligaments are cut to re-align the toe in its proper orientation. After the toe is straightened part of the bone is removed and the incision is closed. The foot can be numbed at the ankle or the patient can be given general anesthesia.
common_complications: Complications include injury to the joint, ligaments, cartilage, nerves or blood vessels. All surgery comes with the risk of infection and blood clots. Patients can infrequently have bad reactions to anesthesia including allergic reactions. The surgery may not relieve the pain or deformity of the foot.

name: Neuroma excision (surgical removal of a swollen nerve)
description: An incision is made over the neuroma and the fibrous nerve tissue is removed. The surgery can be done with local anesthesia by numbing the foot at the ankle or the patient can be given general anesthesia.
common_complications: Complications include injury to the joint, ligaments, cartilage, nerves or blood vessels. All surgery comes with the risk of infection and blood clots. Patients can infrequently have bad reactions to anesthesia including allergic reactions. The surgery may not completely relieve pain.

name: Plantar fasciotomy (surgical cutting of foot ligament)
description: An incision is made over the heel. The inflamed tissue is removed and the plantar fascia is cut from the heel. The foot can be numbed at the ankle or the patient can be given general anesthesia. The procedure is most commonly performed to treat chronic plantar fasciitis.
common_complications: Complications include injury to the joint, ligaments, cartilage, nerves or blood vessels. All surgery comes with the risk of infection and blood clots. Patients can infrequently have bad reactions to anesthesia including allergic reactions. The surgery may not relieve the foot pain.

name: Endoscopic plantar fasciotomy (minimally invasive foot surgery)
description: A tube with a camera (endoscope) is inserted through two small incisions in the foot. The inflamed tissue is removed and the plantar fascia is removed from the heel. It is felt the endoscopic approach enables quicker healing than the open technique which requires a larger incision. The foot can be numbed at the ankle or the patient can be given general anesthesia.
common_complications: Complications include injury to the joint, ligaments, cartilage, nerves or blood vessels. All surgery comes with the risk of infection and blood clots. Patients can infrequently have bad reactions to anesthesia including allergic reactions. The surgery may not relieve the foot pain.

name: Pulmonary function tests (PFTs, measurement of how lungs are working)
description: A group of tests that measure how well the lungs work. The patient breathes into a disposable mouth piece. A technician measures the amount of air that moves in and out of the lungs and how forcefully the patient can push the air out. The tests also measure how well oxygen is delivered to the body and how much carbon dioxide is removed. The tests can help diagnose lung diseases such as asthma, chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD), chronic bronchitis, emphysema, and pulmonary fibrosis.
common_complications: None.

name: Rapid flu test
description: A test that can identify infection with the influenza virus. The test is usually performed in less than an hour. Most tests can detect influenza A and B. A swab or washing of the nasal cavity is usually performed.
common_complications: The test is not always accurate. A person can have influenza and the rapid flu test can be negative.

name: Rapid strep test
description: A swab of the throat that can rapidly detect the presence of a streptococcal infection. The streptococcal bacterium is the organism that causes strep throat.
common_complications: Swabbing the back of the throat can be uncomfortable. The test is not always accurate. A person can have strep throat and the rapid strep may be negative.

name: Panorex (dental x-ray of upper and lower jaw)
description: A special x-ray that takes a panoramic image of the teeth and the jaw. The test is done to identify cavities of the tooth, or problems with the jaw bone such as fractures.
common_complications: Frequent exposure to x-rays has a small risk of radiation induced cancer later in life.

name: Peak expiratory flow rate (PEFR, measurement of airflow through lungs)
description: A breathing test that measures how forcibly air can be exhaled. The test is used to detect obstruction of the airways such as seen in asthma or chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD).
common_complications: None

name: Polysomnography (sleep study)
description: Also called a sleep study. This test measures brain waves, oxygen levels, heart rate, breathing rate, eye movements, and leg movements during sleep. The full test is performed in the hospital or in a sleep center. The test is done to identify sleep apnea, restless leg syndrome, narcolepsy, or problems with REM sleep.
common_complications: None.

name: Tonometry (test to measure pressure inside eye)
description: A test that measures the pressure inside the eye (intraocular pressure). There are multiple methods to measure the pressure including: applanation tonometry, electronic indentation tonometry, pneumotonometry, and indentation tonometry (Schiotz). An elevated intraocular pressure is found in glaucoma. A rise in intraocular can happen without symptoms. Thats why the pressure is measured during a routine eye exam.
common_complications: Minor discomfort.

name: Prothrombin time (PT, blood clotting test)
description: One of the blood tests that measures the blood's ability to clot. A prolonged prothrombin (PT) means that blood clots less readily. The test is most often used to determine the correct dose of warfarin (Coumadin). To standardize the test results around the world, the test is also reported as INR (international normalized ratio). A prolonged PT also occurs in people with advanced liver disease.
common_complications: None.

name: Platelet aggregation test (blood clotting test)
description: A blood test that measures how well platelets clump together and form blood clots. The test will be abnormal if the platelets are diseased or if the patient is taking certain medications, such as aspirin based preparations or nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs.
common_complications: None

name: Progesterone level (blood test measurement of female hormone)
description: Progesterone is a naturally occurring hormone and rises and falls during a woman's menstrual cycle and during pregnancy. A level is often measured during the evaluation of infertility.
common_complications: None

name: Blood cell count (reticulocyte count)
description: A blood test that measures the percentage of red blood cells that are immature cells (reticulocytes). Increased numbers of immature red blood cells indicate that the bone marrow is responding appropriately to anemia. For example, this is seen when a patient loses blood or if red blood cells are destroyed.
common_complications: None.

name: Rheumatoid factor (blood test for autoimmune disease)
description: A blood test that measures the amount of rheumatoid factor antibody in the blood. The test is done to help diagnose rheumatoid arthritis. However, many patients with rheumatoid arthritis have a negative rheumatoid factor level.
common_complications: None.

name: Renal vascular ultrasound (ultrasound of kidney blood vessels)
description: A special ultrasound that evaluates the blood flow through the renal artery supplying the kidneys. If blood flow is decreased because of narrowing of the renal artery, its called renal artery stenosis. The most common cause is hardening of the arteries (atherosclerosis). An ultrasound uses high frequency sound waves to study organs inside the body.
common_complications: None.

name: Skin biopsy (skin sample)
description: A small piece of skin is removed for examination under a microscope. The most common reason for the test is to determine the cause of a rash or diagnose skin cancer. There are 3 types: a shave biopsy takes a thin slice of skin; a punch biopsy uses a circular sharp tool and removes a round section of skin including the deeper layers; an excisional biopsy removes more skin and tissue using a scalpel.
