name: Brain MRI with dye
description: MRI is magnetic resonance imaging, a special imaging test that does not use x-rays. This test provides very detailed images of the brain and surrounding structures. In general a MRI is better than a CT scan at determining acute strokes, infections and tumors. An intravenous dye called gadolinium is used to obtain better images.
common_complications: Gadolinium has been associated with a serious skin and connective tissue disease called nephrogenic systemic fibrosis (NSF).  Patients with chronic kidney disease are at increased risk of developing NSF after gadolinium. More information can be found at http://www.fda.gov/Drugs/DrugSafety/DrugSafetyNewsletter/ucm142889.

name: Brain MRI without dye
description: MRI is magnetic resonance imaging, a special imaging test that does not use x-rays. This test provides very detailed images of the brain and surrounding structures. In general a MRI is better at determining acute strokes, infections and tumors than a CT scan.
common_complications: None

name: Chest MRI without dye
description: MRI is magnetic resonance imaging, a special imaging test that does not use x-rays. It provides very detailed images of the chest, heart, lungs, esophagus and mediastinum.
common_complications: None.

name: Chest MRI with dye
description: MRI is magnetic resonance imaging, a special imaging test that does not use x-rays. It provides very detailed images of the chest, heart, lungs, esophagus and mediastinum. An intravenous dye called gadolinium is used to obtain better images. Chest MRI with dye is usually ordered to look for clots, tears or other abnormalities in blood vessels.
common_complications: Gadolinium has been associated with a serious skin and connective tissue disease called nephrogenic systemic fibrosis (NSF). It appears patients with chronic kidney disease are at increased risk of developing NSF after gadolinium. More information can be found at http://www.fda.gov/Drugs/DrugSafety/DrugSafetyNewsletter/ucm142889.

name: Brain CTA (CT angiogram)
description: A computer enhanced x-ray that enables a doctor to see abnormalities of the brain and blood vessels of the brain. Intravenous dye (contrast) is given when detailed pictures of the arteries in the neck and inside the brain are needed to determine diagnosis and treatment of problems such as aneurysms and arteriovenous malformations (AVMs).
common_complications: CT scans require radiation. Multiple exposures to radiation increase the risk of cancer later in life. The intravenous contrast can injure the kidneys, especially if the person has underlying kidney disease. Some patients can be allergic to the contrast resulting in a rash to life-threatening swelling and low blood pressure.

name: Brain CT (CAT) scan without dye
description: A computer enhanced x-ray that enables a doctor to see abnormalities of the brain. A head CT scan is an excellent test to look for evidence of bleeding in or around the brain. It can be done quickly, which is important when a person has symptoms of an acute stroke (brain attack).
common_complications: CT scans require radiation. Multiple exposures to radiation increase the risk of cancer later in life.

name: Brain CT (CAT) scan with dye
description: A computer enhanced x-ray that enables a doctor to see abnormalities of the brain. Intravenous dye (contrast) is given to provide detailed pictures of blood vessels.
common_complications: CT scans require radiation. Multiple exposures to radiation increase the risk of cancer later in life. The intravenous contrast dye can injure the kidneys, especially if the person has underlying kidney disease. Some patients can be allergic to the contrast resulting in a rash to life-threatening swelling and low blood pressure.

name: Neck CTA (CT image of neck arteries)
description: A computer enhanced x-ray that enables a doctor to see abnormalities of blood vessels of the neck. Intravenous dye (contrast) is given to provide detailed pictures of blood vessels. This test is most often used to detect blocked arteries causing strokes, damaged neck arteries or veins, aneurysms, or blood clots.
common_complications: CT scans require radiation. Multiple exposures to radiation increase the risk of cancer later in life. The intravenous contrast dye can injure the kidneys, especially if the person has underlying kidney disease. Some patients can be allergic to the contrast resulting in a rash to life-threatening swelling and low blood pressure.

name: Lower extremity joint MRI with dye (leg MRI)
description: MRI is magnetic resonance imaging, a special imaging test that does not use x-rays. This test provides very detailed images of the joint and surrounding muscles and bones. This test can help identify arthritis, traumatic injuries, ligament tears, tendon ruptures, meniscus injuries, infections and fractures. An intravenous dye called gadolinium is used to obtain better images.
common_complications: Gadolinium has been associated with a serious skin and connective tissue disease called nephrogenic systemic fibrosis (NSF). It appears patients with chronic kidney disease are at increased risk of developing NSF after gadolinium. More information can be found at http://www.fda.gov/Drugs/DrugSafety/DrugSafetyNewsletter/ucm142889.

name: Upper extremity joint MRI with dye (arm MRI)
description: MRI is magnetic resonance imaging, a special imaging test that does not use x-rays. This test provides very detailed images of the joint and surrounding muscles and bones. This test can help identify arthritis, traumatic injuries, ligament tears, tendon ruptures, infections and fractures. An intravenous dye called gadolinium is used to obtain better images.
common_complications: Gadolinium has been associated with a serious skin and connective tissue disease called nephrogenic systemic fibrosis (NSF). It appears patients with chronic kidney disease are at increased risk of developing NSF after gadolinium. More information can be found at http://www.fda.gov/Drugs/DrugSafety/DrugSafetyNewsletter/ucm142889.

name: Upper extremity joint MRI without dye (arm MRI)
description: MRI is magnetic resonance imaging, a special imaging test that does not use x-rays. This test provides very detailed images of the joint and surrounding muscles and bones. This test can help identify arthritis, traumatic injuries, ligament tears, tendon ruptures, infections and fractures.
common_complications: None.

name: Upper extremity CT scan without dye (arm CAT scan)
description: A test using computer enhanced x-rays that provides detailed images of the bones, tendons, muscles, and joints of the arm.
common_complications: CT scans require radiation. Multiple exposures to radiation increase the risk of cancer later in life.

name: Upper extremity CT scan with dye (arm CAT scan)
description: A test using special x-rays that provides detailed images of the blood vessels, bones, tendons, muscles, and joints of the arm. Dye (contrast) is given in the vein when information regarding blood supply or abnormalities of blood vessels is especially important.
common_complications: CT scans require radiation. Multiple exposures to radiation increase the risk of cancer later in life. The intravenous contrast can injure the kidneys, especially if the person has underlying kidney disease. Some patients can be allergic to the contrast resulting in a rash to life-threatening swelling and low blood pressure.

name: Lower extremity CT scan without dye (leg CAT scan)
description: A test using computer enhanced x-rays that provides detailed images of the bones, tendons, muscles, and joints of the leg.
common_complications: CT scans require radiation. Multiple exposures to radiation increase the risk of cancer later in life.

name: Lower extremity CT scan with dye (leg CAT scan)
description: A test using computer enhanced x-rays that provides detailed images of the blood vessels, bones, tendons, muscles, and joints of the leg. Dye (contrast) is given in the vein when information regarding blood supply or abnormalities of blood vessels is especially important.
common_complications: CT scans require radiation. Multiple exposures to radiation increase the risk of cancer later in life. The intravenous contrast can injure the kidneys, especially if the person has underlying kidney disease. Some patients can be allergic to the contrast resulting in a rash to life-threatening swelling and low blood pressure.

name: Triangular fibrocartilage complex repair (wrist cartilage surgical repair)
description: A surgical procedure to repair a damaged triangular fibrocartilage complex (TFCC). The TFCC is cartilage that acts as a cushion and helps provide support to the wrist where it connects to the forearm bones. The surgeon can do an open or arthroscopic repair. The open repair requires a bigger incision. In the arthroscopic approach, the surgeon can makes a small incision to insert an instrument with a camera to visualize and repair the damage.
common_complications: Complications include injury to the joint, ligaments, cartilage, nerves or blood vessels, and infection. Patients can infrequently have an adverse reaction to anesthesia.

name: Cervical facet joint injection (neck joint injection for pain)
description: A procedure that is used to treat neck pain caused by an irritated nerve near a facet joint in the neck. A needle is inserted near the irritated nerve causing the pain. A local anesthetic and a corticosteroid are injected into the area. The anesthetic usually gives some immediate relief and the corticosteroid may diminish pain for months.
common_complications: Complications include bleeding, infection, allergic reaction, headache, and nerve damage. Nerve damage can result in increased pain, numbness and/or arm weakness.

name: Facet joint injection (spinal injection for pain)
description: A procedure that is used to treat neck or back pain being caused by an irritated nerve near a facet joint of the neck or back. A needle is inserted near the irritated nerve causing the pain. A local anesthetic and a corticosteroid are injected into the area. The anesthetic usually gives some immediate relief and the corticosteroid may diminish pain for months.
common_complications: Complications include bleeding, infection, allergic reaction, headache, and nerve damage. Nerve damage can result in increased pain, numbness and/or weakness of an arm or leg.

name: Thoracic facet joint injection (upper back injection for pain)
description: A procedure that is used to treat mid back pain being caused by an irritated nerve near a facet joint of the mid back. A needle is inserted near the irritated nerve causing the pain. A local anesthetic and a corticosteroid are injected into the area. The anesthetic usually gives some immediate relief and the corticosteroid may diminish pain for months.
common_complications: Complications include bleeding, infection, allergic reaction, headache, and nerve damage. Nerve damage can result in increased pain or numbness.

name: Intrauterine device (IUD, birth control device )
description: An Intrauterine device (IUD) is a form of birth control used by women. Either a copper containing device or a hormone containing device is inserted in the uterus to prevent pregnancy. This procedure is 99.2 to 99.9% effective in preventing pregnancy. IUDs do not protect against sexually transmitted diseases, including HIV.
common_complications: Complications include cramping, bleeding, and pain. Very rarely the IUD pokes a hole in the uterus during placement. If a patient becomes pregnant with an IUD there is an increased risk of having a miscarriage or an ectopic pregnancy.

name: Arthrodesis (joint fusion)
description: Arthrodesis is also called joint fusion. Joint fusion is surgery that decreases the movement of the joint. It can be done on any joint in the body and is usually performed to improve stability and decrease pain.
common_complications: Complications include bleeding, infection, blood clots and reactions to anesthesia. Other complications are dependent on the joint being fused.

name: Flu (influenza) vaccine
description: A vaccine designed to protect against the flu. The flu is caused by the influenza virus and each year experts predict which type of flu virus will be most common. Since the virus may change from one year to the next a new vaccine is needed every fall. The vaccine can protect a patient from getting sick or it can make the illness milder if a person is infected with a related but different influenza strain. The Center for Disease Control (CDC) recommends everyone 6 months and older to get the flu vaccine each year and this should occur before December.
common_complications: The risk of a vaccine causing serious harm or death is extremely rare. The following people should not receive the vaccine: severe allergy to chicken eggs, previous severe reaction to the vaccine, children younger than 6 months, patients with a moderate to severe illness with a fever, and patients with a history of Guillain-Barre syndrome. For more information see http://www.cdc.gov/vaccines

name: HPV (human papiloma virus) vaccine
description: A vaccine designed to protect against contracting HPV, which can help to prevent cervical cancer. There are different types of HPV vaccines available. The vaccine is recommended for girls and boys as young as 11 or 12 years of age, usually given as a 3-dose series. The vaccine is also recommended for females 13-26 and males 13-21 who did not receive all 3 doses when they were younger.
common_complications: These vaccines were not associated with any serious reactions in controlled studies. Less severe reactions that may occur are pain, redness, fever, or other allergic reactions. The following people should not get the vaccine: anyone having a severe reaction to the vaccine in the past, anyone who has had a severe reaction to any vaccine, and people who are significantly sick at the time of the vaccine (it is better to wait until the patient is well). For more information see http://www.cdc.gov/vaccines

name: Hepatitis A vaccine
description: A vaccine designed to protect against the hepatitis A virus. The vaccine is recommended for the following people: all children 12-23 months of age, anyone older than 1 year traveling or living in countries with a high prevalence of hepatitis A (Mexico, Central America, South America, Asia excluding Japan, Africa, Eastern Europe), ages 2-18 years who live in areas of the U.S. with high incidence of the infection, men who have sex with men, intravenous drug users, patients with chronic liver disease, patients receiving clotting factor medications, and family members adopting a child from a region where the disease is common. The vaccine is proven to protect against Hepatitis A virus for at least 10 years. The vaccine is given in 2 divided doses. The initial dose should be followed up with a booster 6-12 months later.
common_complications: The risk of a vaccine causing serious harm or death is extremely rare. Less severe reactions that may occur are pain, redness, fever, or other allergic reactions. The following people should not get the vaccine: anyone having a severe reaction to the vaccine in the past, anyone who has had a severe reaction to any vaccine, and people who are significantly sick at the time of the vaccine (it is better to wait until the patient is well). For more information see http://www.cdc.gov/vaccines

name: Hepatitis B vaccine
description: A vaccine designed to protect against the hepatitis B virus. The vaccine is recommended in all children at birth and any patient who has a high risk of acquiring the infection. The vaccine is given in 3 divided doses before the child reaches 18 months (1 dose at birth, the second dose 1-2 months later, the third dose between 6 and 18 months). The vaccine may be given at the same time as other vaccines.
common_complications: The risk of a vaccine causing serious harm or death is extremely rare. Less severe reactions that may occur are pain, redness, fever, or other allergic reactions. The following people should not receive the vaccine: patients with a severe allergic reaction to yeast, previous severe reaction to the vaccine, and people who are significantly sick at the time of the vaccine (it is better to wait until the patient is well). For more information see http://www.cdc.gov/vaccines

name: Meningitis (meningococcal) vaccine
description: A vaccine designed to protect against the bacteria Neisseria meningitidis (meningococcus). Meningococcus can cause very serious infections involving the blood or brain and spinal cord (meningitis). The vaccine is recommended in all children at the age of 11 or 12 followed by a booster shot at age 16. The following of other groups should receive the vaccine: college students living in close quarters (dormitories), U.S. military recruits, people living in parts of the world with high rates of the disease, patients with a damaged spleen, patients without a spleen, some patients with immune deficiencies, and people who have been exposed to the disease.
common_complications: The risk of a vaccine causing serious harm or death is extremely rare. Less severe reactions that may occur are pain, redness, fever, or other allergic reactions. The following people should not get the vaccine: anyone having a severe reaction to the vaccine in the past, anyone who has had a severe reaction to any vaccine, and people who are significantly sick at the time of the vaccine (it is better to wait until the patient is well). For more information see http://www.cdc.gov/vaccines

name: Pneumococcal (pneumonia) vaccine
description: A vaccine designed to protect against the bacteria Streptococcus pneumoniae (pneumococcus). Pneumococcus is one of the bacteria that can cause pneumonia. There are two types of vaccine: pneumococcal conjugate vaccine (PCV13) and pneumococcal polysaccharide vaccine (PPSV). The following patients should receive PCV13: infants and children less than 2 years old, children 2-5 years old who are not adequately vaccinated, children 6-18 years old with higher risks of infection (sickle cell disease, HIV-infection, other immune compromising diseases, cochlear implant, or cerebrospinal fluid leaks). The following patients should receive both PCV13 and PPSV: all people over 65, patients 2-64 years old with a disease that lowers their immune system, patients 19-64 years old who have asthma or smoke, and people who live in nursing homes or long term care facilities. The two vaccines should not be given at the same visit and when possible PCV13 should be given first and PPSV at a later date.
common_complications: The risk of a vaccine causing serious harm or death is extremely rare. Less severe reactions that may occur are pain, redness, fever, or other allergic reactions. The following people should not get the vaccine: anyone having a severe reaction to the vaccine in the past, anyone who has had a severe reaction to any vaccine, and people who are significantly sick at the time of the vaccine (it is better to wait until the patient is well). For more information see http://www.cdc.gov/vaccines

name: Chicken pox (varicella) vaccine
description: A vaccine designed to protect against the Varicella virus. The vaccine is recommended for all children under 13 and for everyone 13 or older who has never had chickenpox. The vaccine is divided in two doses recommended to be given at 12 to 15 months and a second dose at age 4 to 6 years.
common_complications: The risk of a vaccine causing serious harm or death is extremely rare. Less severe reactions that may occur are pain, redness, fever, or other allergic reactions. The following people should not get the vaccine: anyone having a severe reaction to the vaccine in the past, people who are significantly sick at the time of the vaccine (it is better to wait until the patient is well), and pregnant patients (they should wait until after having the baby). Any patient with a weakened immune system should contact their doctor before receiving the vaccine. For more information see http://www.cdc.gov/vaccines

name: Tetanus vaccine (Td vaccine)
description: A vaccine designed to protect against tetanus infections. Tetanus vaccine can be given alone. However, it is most often given with a vaccine against diphtheria and sometimes against pertussis. The booster vaccine is recommended every 10 years starting at age 19. Individuals who have sustained puncture type wounds should also receive the booster if it has been more than 10 years since the last booster. Patients who have experienced a dirty or contaminated wound will need a booster if their last vaccine was more than 5 years ago.
common_complications: The risk of a vaccine causing serious harm or death is extremely rare. Less severe reactions that may occur are pain, redness, fever, or other allergic reactions. The following people should not get the vaccine: anyone having a severe reaction to the vaccine in the past, any child who has had a brain or nervous system disorder within 7 days after a previous vaccine, and people who are significantly sick at the time of the vaccine (it is better to wait until the patient is well). For more information see http://www.cdc.gov/vaccines

name: Shingles vaccine
description: A vaccine designed to protect against the herpes zoster (shingles) virus. The shingles vaccine can also reduce the severity of symptoms in people who still get the virus. A single dose of the shingles vaccine is recommended for adults 60 years of age and older. Scientific studies show the vaccine reduces the risk of developing shingles by about 50%.
common_complications: The risk of a vaccine causing serious harm or death is extremely rare. Less severe reactions that may occur are pain, redness, fever, or other allergic reactions. The following people should not get the vaccine: anyone having a severe reaction to the vaccine in the past, anyone who has had a severe reaction to neomycin or gelatin, patients with a weakened immune system, and people who are significantly sick at the time of the vaccine (it is better to wait until the patient is well). For more information see http://www.cdc.gov/vaccines

name: Camp physical
description: A camp physical is an exam that helps to determine the health of the individual before attending the camp and an opportunity to discuss important health issues with parents and children. There are two main parts to a camp physical which are obtaining a detailed medical history and a physical exam.  The physical may vary depending on the requirements set forth by the requested organization. The physicals are required yearly.
common_complications: None

name: School physical
description: A school physical is an exam that helps to determine the health of the individual before attending the school and an opportunity to discuss important health issues with parents and children. There are two main parts to a school physical which are obtaining a detailed medical history and a physical exam.  The physical may vary depending on the requirements set forth by the requested organization. The frequency of physicals is determined by the primary care clinician.
common_complications: None

name: Sports physical
description: A sports physical is an exam that helps to determine the health of the individual before participating in sports and an opportunity to discuss important health issues with parents and children.  There are two main parts to a sports physical, which are obtaining a detailed medical history and a physical exam.  The physical may vary depending on the requirements set forth by the requested organization. The physicals are usually done yearly.
common_complications: None

name: Blood pressure screening
description: Blood pressure screening should begin at age 18 according to recommendations by the U.S. Preventive Services Task Force.  Blood pressure is measured by two numbers. The top number is called the systolic which is the pressure in the blood vessels when the heart beats. The bottom number is called the diastolic which is the pressure in the blood vessel between heart beats. Normal blood pressure is the systolic number 120 or less over the diastolic number 80 or less. Blood pressure checks should be done at least once every 2 years when blood pressure is less than 120/80 and at least yearly if 120- 139/80-89.
common_complications: None

name: Health screening
description: Health screening is a test or exam to find a condition before symptoms begin. Screening tests may help find diseases or conditions early, when they are easier to treat. Recommended screening tests or exams vary depending on your gender, age, family history and risk factors for diseases.
common_complications: None

name: Employment physical
description: An employment physical is an exam that helps to determine the health of the individual and to determine if the individual is fit to perform the tasks required by him or her to complete the job duties outlined by the employer.  There are two main parts to an employment physical which are obtaining a detailed medical history and a physical exam.  The physical exam may vary depending on the requirements set forth by the requested organization. The frequency of physicals is determined by the employer.
common_complications: None

name: Breathing treatment with nebulizer
description: A nebulizer is a device that delivers asthma or COPD (Chronic Obstructive Pulmonary Disease) medication directly into the lungs. The nebulizer machine turns the liquid medication into a mist that is inhaled into the lungs of an individual who may be having breathing difficulty and /or if the individual is having a difficult time with using an inhaler. The individual receiving the breathing treatment often uses a facemask for the mist to enter the lungs. Nebulizer treatments are used on all age groups, but most often on infants and children. Each breathing treatment may last 5-10 minutes or longer.
common_complications: Sore or dry throat, headaches, nausea, vomiting or nervousness. In rare cases, individuals being treated for respiratory problems may experience worse symptoms following the breathing treatment.

name: Ear wax removal
description: Ear wax removal may be necessary when too much wax builds up in the ear canal leading to ear pain, ear fullness and/or decreased hearing. Removal of the ear wax may start with softening of the ear wax with a few drops of mineral oil or hydrogen peroxide to allow for the loosened wax to work its way out naturally. Gentle irrigation with water may also be necessary with a bulb syringe. If your ear continues to be impacted with ear wax, your provider may use a curette with or without a microscope to remove the impacted ear wax.
common_complications: Pain, infection, and bleeding may occur of the inner ear skin or ear drum. In rare cases eardrum perforation or hearing loss may occur.

name: Splinter removal
description: A splinter is a small sliver of wood. The size and location of the splinter will determine the splinter removal method. Most superficial splinters may be removed by individuals themselves. Deeper or more difficult splinters may need to be removed by the provider. The area surrounding the splinter will be thoroughly cleansed to limit the chance of any infection. The medical provider use forceps or other devices to grab the splinter to remove from the skin. If the splinter is deep a local anesthetic may be applied to limit the pain during the procedure. A small incision may also be required to retrieve the splinter. When possible a splinter should be removed as soon as possible to prevent skin swelling and redness (inflammation), or an infection.
common_complications: If the splinter is not removed completely, complications may occur such as inflammation of the skin and surrounding tissue and infection.

name: Staple or suture removal
description: Staples or sutures may be left in place from 5-14 days on average depending on the location and the size of the wound. Your healthcare provider will give you specific instructions on the length the staples or sutures are needed to be left in place based on your individual wound. The wound should be cleaned prior to the removal of the sutures or staples. Staples are generally removed using a sterile staple extractor, while sutures are removed using a combination of a forceps or tweezers with scissors. Once the staples or sutures are removed the wound is cleaned again and a dressing is applied over the wound.
common_complications: If the wound has healed without any symptoms or signs of infection or inflammation, suture or staple removal is almost always uneventful. However, there is always a possibility that a wound could reopen or sutures/staples could be hidden and left in the skin.

name: Diabetes screening
description: Screening to determine if an individual has pre-diabetes or diabetes can be done with one of three different tests called fasting blood glucose, oral glucose tolerance test or with a blood test for hemoglobin A1C. The American Diabetes Association recommends routine screening for diabetes to begin at approximately age 45. Screening should begin at a younger age for people at higher than average risk for diabetes, such as being obese or having a family history of diabetes.
common_complications: None

name: Medication renewal
description: A convenient service to help patients not miss any doses or suffer interruption in their medication schedule. Its called medication adherence. The clinician indicates the number of refills when the prescription is initially written.
common_complications: Certain medications may not be eligible for the service, such as narcotics, medications that may interact with other medications the individual is taking, or medications that need prior authorization to fill.

name: Rotavirus vaccine
description: Rotavirus is the most common cause of severe vomiting and diarrhea in children. There are two vaccines RotaTeq/RV5 and Rotarix/RV1, both have been shown to be effective and relatively safe in preventing the great majority of rotavirus illnesses. The vaccine dose and schedule is dependent on the type given and is given in 2-3 doses (1 dose each at 2, 4 and 6 months of age).
common_complications: A small number of infants may experience fussiness, diarrhea and/or vomiting. Babies with the following conditions should not receive the vaccine: history of severe allergic reactions to the vaccine or to latex; those with a decreased immune system from diseases, cancer, medications, or other medical treatments such as radiation therapy; those who are currently suffering from a moderate to severe rotavirus infection; and those with a history of an intestinal disease called intussusception. For more information see http://www.cdc.gov/vaccines

name: Polio vaccine
description: The polio vaccine protects patients against the polio virus. Prior to the discovery of the vaccine, polio was a common disease worldwide, including the United States. Widespread immunization has made this a rare disease. There are 2 types of vaccines, an inactivated polio vaccine (IPV) and an oral polio vaccine (OPV). In the U.S., only the inactivated vaccine is used. It is given as an injection and is administered as 4 doses (at 2 months, 4 months, 6 -18 months and 4-6 years of age). IPV can be given with other vaccines. OPV is still used in other parts of the world.
common_complications: IPV is generally considered safe. But it should be avoided in people with a history of severe allergic reaction to the vaccine; with a history of severe reaction to the antibiotics neomycin, streptomycin or polymyxin B; or who are moderately to severely ill at the time the vaccine was scheduled. For more information see http://www.cdc.gov/vaccines

name: Haemophilus influenza type B (Hib) vaccine
description: This vaccine protects patients against the serious infection caused by the Haemophilus influenzae type b (Hib) bacteria. This infection most often affects children less than 5 years old and can cause pneumonia, epiglottitis, and infections involving the heart, joints, bones, and blood stream. The vaccine should be given in 3-4 doses, with the first 2 doses at 2 months and 4 months. Depending on the brand of vaccine, at least one additional dose is given before 15 months.
common_complications: The vaccine is generally considered safe. But patients with a history of severe allergic reactions to this vaccine and those who are moderately to severely ill at the time of scheduled vaccination should not receive this vaccine. For more information see http://www.cdc.gov/vaccines

name: Gram Stain
description: A gram stain is a test used to identify bacteria. Lab technicians place a thin layer of a sample on a microscope slide and apply a series of stains. The color, size, and shape of the cells are some qualities used to determine the type of bacteria. Samples can be obtained from bodily fluids or tissue from a biopsy.
common_complications: None

name: Iron level
description: Iron is a mineral that is an essential component of red blood cells. An iron level measures the amount of iron in the blood. Low levels of iron may be a cause of anemia.
common_complications: None

name: Fungal test (KOH Prep)
description: A KOH test is a lab test that identifies fungus. A sample, such as a skin scraping, is placed on a microscope slide. Then, potassium hydroxide (KOH) is applied to the sample, destroying all material other than fungal cells. The fungal cells are then visible to the laboratory technician under the microscope.
common_complications: None

name: Throat culture
description: A throat culture is a lab test that checks for bacterial or fungal infections of the throat. The most common bacterial infection is due to group A streptococcus (strep throat). A throat culture is performed by using a sterile cotton swab and rubbing it against the back of the throat. The sample is then placed in a special container and incubated for 18-48 hours. If nothing grows, the culture is considered "negative". If there is growth, the lab technician will identify the type of bacteria or fungus present.
common_complications: Complications may include gagging, mild pain or discomfort.  When performed properly, the accuracy of a throat culture to determine if you have strep throat is about 95%.

name: Transesophageal echocardiogram (TEE)
description: Transesophageal echocardiogram is an imaging study that uses ultrasound (sound waves that create a picture) to study the heart's position, motion of the walls, and valves. The test involves a flexible tube with an ultrasound transducer tip that is placed down the throat and into the esophagus. This test provides a more detailed picture of the heart than a standard echocardiogram because the rib cage is not in the way.  This test can be used most often to look at the heart valves for evidence of infection (called endocarditis). It can also help diagnose an enlarged heart, other valve disorders, weakened heart muscle and blood clots inside the heart.
common_complications: Transesophageal echocardiogram has a relatively low risk of complications. Occasionally, the medication that helps relax the body during the procedure may produce nausea, trouble breathing or an allergic reaction. Some individuals may experience a sore throat for a few hours after the test.  Rarely, the probe may damage the esophagus.

name: Blood type, screen, and crossmatch
description: Blood typing is a lab test that identifies a person's specific red blood cell type. Blood types are based on the ABO system. There are a variety of proteins (antigens) on the outside of red blood cells and blood typing defines these proteins and gives the blood type a name (A positive, O negative, etc). Cross matching takes this process one step further and identifies minor proteins that are different than those defined in the typing procedure. Together with typing, cross-matched blood assures compatibility during a transfusion. Blood typing and cross-matching are frequently performed prior to surgery, or when a blood transfusion is anticipated.
common_complications: None

name: Thyroid ultrasound
description: Thyroid ultrasonography is a diagnostic imaging test of the thyroid. During the exam, the ultrasound probe is pressed against the front of the neck. Sound waves from the device bounce off tissues and create echoes which are turned into pictures. A thyroid ultrasound is most often performed to evaluate an enlarged thyroid or a lump felt by the doctor during a physical exam. Most lumps are benign nodules. Sometimes a lump may be a cyst.
common_complications: None

name: Uric acid level
description: A uric acid level is a blood test that measures the chemical that is left after the body breaks down purines. Purines are natural substances that are present throughout the body and in many foods. A high blood uric acid increases the risk of gout and kidney damage.
common_complications: None

name: Urine culture
description: A urine culture is a lab test that checks for bacterial or fungal infections in the urine. Urine is usually collected with a method called a "clean catch". To avoid contamination, you wipe the genital area first and then capture the urine in a sterile cup. A catheter is sometimes used to obtain a sample. The sample is then placed in a special container and incubated for 18-48 hours. If nothing grows, the culture is considered "negative". If there is growth, the lab technician will identify the type of bacteria or fungus present.
common_complications: None

name: Vaginal wet prep/culture
description: A clinician will perform a pelvic exam to obtain a sample of vaginal fluid. A drop of the fluid can be placed on a slide to identify certain infections such as trichomonas and bacterial vaginosis. This is known as a wet prep. If needed, the rest of the sample may be placed in a special container and sent to the lab for culture. This can detect other types of bacterial, parasitic or fungal infections in the vagina. The sample is incubated for 18-48 hours. If nothing grows, the culture is considered "negative". If there is growth, the lab technician will identify the type of bacteria, parasite or fungus present.
common_complications: None although there may be minor vaginal discomfort during the pelvic exam.

name: Wood's light analysis
description: Wood's light analysis is a test that utilizes a handheld black light. The light is held 4-5 inches over the skin in a dark room. Normally, your skin will not change color under the ultraviolet light. If your skin does shine under the light, it may indicate a fungal or bacterial infection of the skin.
common_complications: None

name: Chest x-ray
description: A diagnostic imaging test that shows an x-ray image of the chest, lungs, ribs, heart, large arteries and diaphragm. Chest x-rays are most often done to help diagnose a lung infection, to look for a large heart or fluid in the lung, or to help determine the reason for a persistent cough or shortness of breath.
common_complications: A chest x-ray requires only a small amount of radiation and is considered safe if performed infrequently. Women who may be pregnant should always inform the doctor and x-ray technician prior to having it done.

name: Fasting blood sugar (glucose)
description: Fasting blood glucose is a blood test that measures the glucose (sugar) level of the blood prior to your first meal. No food or drink is suggested for 10-12 hours prior to the test.  This test is often performed to screen for diabetes.
common_complications: None

name: Semen analysis
description: Semen analysis is a laboratory test that evaluates the quality and quantity of a man's sperm. The most common reason to perform the test is to determine whether a man will have trouble fathering a child (infertility). It is also used to determine the effectiveness of a vasectomy. Test results include sperm concentration (amount), motility (movement) of the sperm, morphology (shape) of the sperm cells, pH and agglutination of sperm (clumping of sperm).
common_complications: None

name: Cold agglutinins
description: A blood test for cold agglutinins looks for the presence of a type of protein that causes red cells to clump together when exposed to a cool temperature. They are sometimes produced by the immune system in response to an infection, such as an infection caused by an organism called Mycoplasma.
common_complications: None

name: Basic metabolic panel (BMP, Chem-7)
description: A Basic Metabolic Panel (BMP or Chem-7) is a blood test that measures the levels of seven blood chemistries. Its one of the most commonly used blood tests to help diagnose and monitor many conditions, including diabetes, kidney disease and acid/base abnormalities. The Chem-7 tests for electrolytes (sodium, potassium, chloride and bicarbonate), kidney function (creatinine, blood urea nitrogen), and glucose (sugar).
common_complications: None

name: Anterior cruciate ligament (ACL) reconstruction
description: ACL reconstruction is a surgical procedure to rebuild the anterior cruciate ligament (ACL) in the center of the knee. The ACL keeps the shin bone in place. This surgery is usually done under general anesthesia. Tissue for the ACL repair is either taken from your own body (hamstring or knee cap tendon) or from a donor. This surgery is usually performed with knee arthroscopy (using small incisions and a scope).
common_complications: Complications include injury to the joint, ligaments, cartilage, nerves or blood vessels. All surgery comes with the risk of infection and blood clots. Patients can infrequently have bad reactions to anesthesia.

name: Core biopsy
description: Core biopsy is a procedure done under local anesthesia where a needle is passed through the skin and into a mass or lump to obtain a sample of the tissue. The needle is hollow and the sample of cells is collected into the hollow needle. The tissue is then examined under a microscope to find any abnormality. Most often, core biopsies are done for breast masses or lumps.
common_complications: Complications occur rarely but may include moving abnormal cells into unaffected tissue when the needle is removed. Some individuals may experience a small amount of pain. There is also the risk of scarring or infection.

name: Cancer antigen 125 (CA-125)
description: A CA-125 blood test is used to help diagnose and manage ovarian cancer. Elevated serum CA-125 levels are associated with ovarian carcinoma of epithelial origin in approximately 80% of women. Levels may be elevated in other cancers as well. Declining CA-125 levels usually correlate with treatment response. The test is not accurate enough to be used for routine ovarian screening of the general population. However, high-risk individuals may undergo CA-125 screening regularly.
common_complications: There are no significant complications of the CA-125 blood test. However, the test has poor sensitivity and specificity.  So, it is not a useful screening test for ovarian cancer. Also, a high CA-125 by itself cannot be used to diagnose ovarian cancer.

name: H. pylori blood antibody test
description: A Helicobacter pylori (H. pylori) antibody test is a blood test which checks for a present or past infection (antibodies to H. pylori).  This blood test is unable to determine if the infection has resolved after being treated. The presence of H. pylori antibodies may not mean you have a current infection but means you have been exposed/infected at some point with H. Pylori. This test may be useful for people with upper abdominal pain. If antibodies are present in the blood, treating the infection may relieve symptoms.
common_complications: None

name: Urea breath test (H. pylori)
description: The urea breath test is a test which determines if you are infected with the H. pylori bacteria.  Typically, you are advised to be off antibiotics, bismuth medication (Pepto-Bismol) and proton pump inhibitors (PPI) for two weeks prior to the test.  During the test, you will swallow a tagged urea substance which will change to ammonia and carbon dioxide if you have an active H. pylori infection.  This test will measure the carbon dioxide in your exhaled breath after 10 minutes of swallowing the substance.  This test is used to diagnose the infection and/or confirm treatment of an H. pylori infection after treatment. A normal result does not contain tagged carbon dioxide as compared with an abnormal result which does contain tagged carbon dioxide.
common_complications: None

name: Valsalva's maneuver
description: A maneuver that is performed by forcibly exhaling against a closed airway. It is done to help diagnose the cause of a heart murmur during the physical exam. This maneuver increases the pressure in the thoracic cavity with a resultant decrease in the venous blood return to the heart. The decreased blood return causes a decrease in the amount of blood pumped by the heart. The person experiences a decrease in blood pressure, light-headedness and possibly fainting.
common_complications: Complications may be due to low blood pressure, which could include lightheadedness and possibly fainting.  Precautions should be taken before performing The Valsalva maneuver should be done with the person sitting or lying down.

name: VQ scan (lung ventilation perfusion scan)
description: A ventilation perfusion lung scan (V/Q scan) is a nuclear medicine imaging test. The test looks at both the air flow through the lungs (ventilation) and blood flow through the lungs (perfusion). In the first part of the test, radioactive albumin is injected into a vein and an image is taken while you lie on a mobile table. The second part of the test involves inhaling radioactive gas through a mask while another image is taken. A radiologist then compares the two images and interprets them. V/Q scans are most often performed to look for a blood clot in the lung (pulmonary embolism).
common_complications: A V/Q scan requires a small amount of radiation exposure, similar to an x-ray. A needle stick is required so there may be some pain and a very small risk of infection. The radioisotopes used for the injection and breathing parts of the test contain radioactive material that evaporates very quickly. Therefore, the radiation risk is minimal but caution is advised for pregnant or breast-feeding women.

name: Alveoloplasty
description: Alveoloplasty is a type of surgery that smooths the jawbone in areas where teeth have been removed or lost. It also is done in preparation for temporary or permanent dentures. This procedure is also called alveoplasty. Alveoloplasty can be done alone. However, it is usually done at the same time that teeth are extracted. Oral and maxillofacial surgeons usually perform alveoloplasties. Some general dentists also do them. Local anesthesia, IV sedation (medicine given in a vein), or general anesthesia may be used. To perform an alveoloplasty, the surgeon first makes a cut in the gum to expose the bone. The necessary bone is removed with instruments and sometimes a rotary drill. A file is used to smooth the bone. Then the gums are stitched closed, typically with dissolvable sutures.
common_complications: After the procedure, the area will be sore for about a week. Some swelling and bruising may occur. Risks include excessive bleeding, infection, or injury to the nerve that provides feeling to the lips and chin. Call your surgeon if you have significant bleeding or swelling, signs of infection such as fever or chills, or loosening of stiches.

name: Crown Lengthening
description: Crown lengthening is a common procedure performed to expose more tooth above the gum line. This is done when a tooth needs a filling or crown, but not enough of the tooth is showing. Crown lengthening is done by a periodontist. This is a dentist who specializes in gum disease. A local anesthetic is used to numb the area. The periodontist will make cuts that pull the gums away from the teeth. Sometimes it's enough to remove only gum tissue. But usually bone that surrounds the tooth must be removed as well. Once enough of the tooth is exposed, the gums are put back in place using a surgical dressing or are stitched together.
common_complications: Usually, the treated area may be sore or bleed for about a week after the procedure. The treated teeth may be more sensitive to heat or cold. This usually goes away with time. There is a risk of an infection developing after surgery. Contact your periodontist if you have bleeding that doesnt stop, if you think the area may be infected, or if you notice tender lumps beneath the lower jaw or in the neck. Gums should usually heal for a couple of months before placement of a permanent crown or filling.

name: Frenectomy
description: A frenectomy is a procedure to remove a fold of mouth tissue called a frenum. Frenums are found between the upper two front teeth, under the tongue, and on the sides of the gums. A frenum is removed when it causes problems. A frenectomy can be performed in a hospital operating room under general anesthesia or in a dental office under local anesthesia. The surgery can be done in as little as 10 to 15 minutes.
common_complications: A frenectomy generally heals without problems and with little pain. Bleeding and infection are a risk of any procedure, but are rare after a frenectomy. In rare cases, a frenectomy in the lower jaw can bruise a nerve and cause numbness in the lower lip and chin. This can last several months.

name: Gingival Flap Surgery
description: Gingival flap surgery is used to treat gum disease. Usually, this procedure is done if scaling and root planing, or deep cleaning, does not eliminate the gum infection. Gingival flap surgery is done by a periodontist. This is a dentist who specializes in gum disease. First the area will be numbed. The periodontist will separate the gums from the teeth in order to access the roots and bone. Inflamed tissue will be removed from between the teeth and from any holes in the bone. Then the root surfaces will be thoroughly cleaned. Another procedure may be done at the same time to repair bone defects. The gums will then be put back over the treated area and stitched in place. An antiseptic mouth rinse is usually prescribed for a couple of weeks.
common_complications: Some bleeding, swelling or discomfort is normal after the procedure. It is important to keep the mouth as clean as possible during the healing period to prevent infection. The treated teeth may become more sensitive to heat or cold. Gums in the area may recede over time. Contact your periodontist if bleeding does not stop or if pain and swelling get worse several days after surgery.

name: Gingivectomy and Gingivoplasty
description: Gingivectomy is the removal of gum tissue by surgery. It is usually performed to remove overgrown gum tissue or gaps (pockets) between the teeth and gums. The procedure can improve how the gums look and make them easier to keep clean. Gingivoplasty is used to change the shape of gums when they are unusual or have formed abnormally.  Gingivectomy and gingivoplasty procedures are both done by a periodontist. This is a dentist who specializes in gum disease. A local anesthetic is used to numb the area. After the gums have been reshaped, a surgical dressing may be used to cover the area. An antiseptic mouth rinse may be prescribed until regular brushing and flossing can resume at the area of surgery.
common_complications: There are no major risks to either procedure. Infection may occur, but it is unusual. Normally, the affected area may ooze blood for the first 24 to 48 hours. After that, it should not bleed much. Contact your periodontist if you have bleeding that doesnt stop, if you think the area may be infected, or if you notice tender lumps beneath the lower jaw or in the neck.

name: Hemisection
description: Hemisection is the process of separating a tooth with two roots into two halves. This procedure is done when decay or bone loss from periodontal disease extends into the area between the roots. A hemisection provides easier access to this area, so it can be treated and kept clean. After numbing the affected area, the dentist will make a cut and separate the gums from the bone. This exposes the roots and the area between them. The dentist will then separate the tooth into two halves and remove any decay from the tooth or roots. Each half of the tooth may be covered with a temporary crown. Root canal therapy will be needed before the final crowns are put in place. A hemisection usually takes 60 minutes. It may take longer if  periodontal disease or decay is severe.
common_complications: Swelling, light bleeding and discomfort are normal after a hemisection. An antiseptic mouth rinse is usually prescribed until normal brushing and flossing can resume.  After a few months, the area should have healed well enough for placement of permanent crowns. The two teeth that result from hemisection will have less bone support than the original tooth. Discuss with your periodontist the prospects of long-term success of this procedure, as well as other options.

name: Molar Uprighting
description: Molar uprighting corrects a tilted molar. A molar can tilt out of position if a tooth next to it is removed. A tilted molar can cause food to get stuck between teeth. Chewing can make tilting worse and destroy the bone in front of the tooth. Before molar uprighting, the dentist will plan the treatment using plaster casts or models of the teeth, photographs and X-rays. Molar uprighting is done using braces. This procedure takes a few months to a year. The amount of time depends on how severely the tooth is tilted. After the molar has been uprighted, a dental implant or bridge may be used to replace the missing tooth.
common_complications: Normally, there is discomfort for a few days after the braces are placed. There may also be discomfort when adjustments are made. The braces may cause irritation. This will usually disappear after a few days. Tooth decay and gum disease can occur if teeth are not brushed and flossed regularly. Contact your dentist if irritation or discomfort lasts longer than a week, or if your braces or appliance break.

name: Sinus Lift
description: A sinus lift is surgery that adds bone to the upper jaw in the area of the molars and premolars. Some people need this procedure before they can get dental implants in the upper jaw. A sinus lift is sometimes called a sinus augmentation. The bone is added between the jaw and the maxillary sinuses, which are on either side of the nose. To make room for the bone, the sinus membrane has to be moved upward, or "lifted." A sinus lift usually is done by a specialist. This could be either an oral and maxillofacial surgeon or a periodontist. Sinus lifts have become common during the last 15 years as more people get dental implants to replace missing teeth.
common_complications: The main risk of a sinus lift is that the sinus membrane could be punctured or torn. If the membrane is torn, the surgeon will either stitch the tear or place a patch over it. If the repair is not successful, the surgeon may stop the procedure and give the hole time to heal. Infection occurs very rarely after sinus lifts. Implants may be placed four to nine months after sinus lift surgery.

name: Whitening
description: Whitening lightens teeth and helps to remove stains and discoloration. It is a popular cosmetic dental procedure, performed by most dentists. To maintain the bright white color, the procedure will need to be repeated. There are two main types of whitening procedures. Vital whitening is performed on teeth that have live nerves. A bleaching product that contains some form of hydrogen peroxide is applied to the tooth surface. In the dentist's office, the bleaching gel is activated by a specialized light or laser so teeth get white faster. Non-vital whitening is done on a tooth that has had root-canal treatment and no longer has a live nerve. The whitening agent is applied inside the tooth. Only dentists can perform non-vital whitening. But vital whitening can be done either in the dentist's office or at home. Products bought over the counter contain a weaker whitening agent than those used in the dentist's office. Therefore, whitening may take longer. A dentist also can make a custom mouthpiece and supply bleaching gel to use at home.
common_complications: Tooth whitening is unlikely to cause serious side effects. The teeth and gums may become more sensitive for a short while. Women should not have teeth whitened while pregnant.

name: Bone Grafts (Dental)
description: A bone graft is used to recreate bone and soft tissue lost due to gum (periodontal) disease, cavities or dental infections. A bone graft is also called regenerative surgery. It's usually done by a specialist, such as an oral and maxillofacial surgeon or a periodontist. These procedures can be performed in a dental office with local anesthesia, or by an oral surgeon using IV sedation (medicine given in a vein). The specialist begins by separating the gums from the teeth. Then the affected area is thoroughly cleaned and holes in the bone are filled with bone or synthetic glasses. The bone is covered with a barrier of skin or a synthetic material. Then the gums are stitched back in place. During the next three to six months, the body fills in the treated area with new bone and soft tissue.
common_complications: Normally, there is some swelling and bleeding of the treated area. The treated teeth or area may become more sensitive to heat and cold. Gums may recede over time. Any exposed tooth roots may develop cavities. It is important to keep the mouth as clean as possible during recovery to help prevent infection. Contact your dentist if bleeding does not stop or if pain and swelling get worse one week after surgery.

name: Gum Graft
description: Gum grafts are used to cover exposed tooth roots in an area where the gums have receded (pulled away from the teeth). Gums can recede because of gum (periodontal) disease, naturally thin gum tissue, or trauma. Gum grafts help prevent further recession. This can stop sensitivity and improve the look of a tooth. Soft tissue used for gum grafts may be taken from the roof of the mouth or from the gum around a nearby tooth. A local anesthetic is used to numb this "donor" area and the area that will receive the graft.  Then the desired amount of tissue is removed from the donor area and stitched into place at the new location. The site is usually covered with a surgical dressing. The donor area is also closed with stitches. Antiseptic mouth rinses are usually prescribed until normal brushing and flossing can begin again.
common_complications: Typically, there are no long-term side effects after a gum-graft procedure. Swelling, discomfort and bleeding from the surgical areas are common during the first couple of weeks after the procedure. Risks include infection and graft rejection. Keeping the mouth clean is important. Sometimes the new gum tissue may need to be reshaped. This procedure is called gingivoplasty.

name: Osseous Surgery
description: Osseous surgery reshapes the bone that holds one or more teeth in place. This procedure eliminates deep pockets and bone defects caused by periodontitis, a form of gum disease.  Osseous surgery is often used to treat bone loss around multiple teeth. It is usually done by a periodontist, a dentist who specializes in gum disease. Before the procedure, a local anesthetic is used to numb the area. To access the roots and bone, the periodontist will cut the gum tissue away from each tooth being treated. The roots will be cleaned and the bone will be reshaped using a hand-held drill. The dentist will then stitch the gums back into place. An antiseptic mouth rinse is usually prescribed until normal brushing and flossing can resume.
common_complications: Normally, there is some bleeding and swelling after the surgery. The treated teeth may become more sensitive to heat and cold. Gums in the area may recede over time. It is important to keep the mouth as clean as possible during the healing period to help prevent infection. Contact your periodontist if bleeding does not stop or if pain and swelling get worse one week after surgery.

name: Root Resection
description: During root resection, one or more roots of a tooth are removed. This procedure is done when bone loss from periodontal (gum) disease extends into the area between the roots and deep periodontal pockets have formed. Severe tooth decay that cannot be treated also may require removing a root. Root resection involves cutting into the inside of the tooth, where there are blood vessels and nerves. For this reason, the remaining roots will need root canal treatment. To perform a root resection, the dentist will numb the area and then separate the gums from the tooth to expose the roots. After removing the affected root(s), the dentist will make sure those that remain are smooth and clean on the outside. Then the gums will be stitched back into place. An antiseptic mouth rinse is usually prescribed until normal brushing and flossing can resume.
common_complications: There may be some discomfort, swelling and light bleeding for a few days. Risks include infection, accidental damage to nearby teeth, or a hole in the sinus for root resection on an upper molar. Root resections are done less often than in the past because other options, such as dental implants, are available. Discuss treatment options with your dentist.

name: Scaling and Root Planing
description: Scaling and root planing is the most common and conservative form of treatment for periodontal (gum) disease. Scaling is the removal of calculus (commonly called tartar) and plaque that attach to the tooth surfaces. Scaling especially targets the area below the gum line, along the root. Plaque is more likely to stick to rough surfaces.  For this reason, the root surface is also made smooth in a process called root planing. Scaling and root planing usually requires more than one visit. Typically, each visit may target one-quarter or one-half of the mouth.
common_complications: The mouth may be sore and teeth may be sensitive to heat and cold for several days or weeks after treatment. Some bleeding may occur as well. The gums will shrink (recede) after successful treatment. This exposes part of the root and may increase the risk of root cavities.

name: Bonding
description: Bonding is a procedure that uses a tooth-colored composite resin (plastic) to repair a tooth. Bonding can be used on teeth that are decayed, chipped, broken or discolored. Bonding is one of the easiest and least costly cosmetic dental treatments. Unlike veneers, it can be done in a single visit. The procedure usually takes 30 to 60 minutes. Bonding of multiple teeth may require several visits. Bonding is applied in layers. Each layer is hardened by an ultraviolet light or laser. Depending on the size and depth of the cavity, anesthesia  may not be needed.
common_complications: Bonded teeth can easily be stained for the first 48 hours after bonding is applied. Avoid tea, coffee, cigarette smoke and other staining substances during this time. Bonding usually lasts several years before needing repair. However, bonding material may chip due to biting or chewing habits. Contact your dentist if you notice sharp edges on your teeth, if the teeth feel strange when you bite down, or if the bonding chips.

name: Fluoride Treatments and Supplements
description: Fluoride is used to strengthen teeth and prevent tooth decay. Dental-office fluoride treatments are commonly given to children as their teeth are developing. Fluoride treatments help to prevent decay in both children and adults. Anyone who is at risk of dental decay can benefit from fluoride treatments. Topical fluoride treatments are applied directly to the teeth, often in the form of a gel, foam or varnish. Fluoride supplements can be prescribed to children who are at high risk of dental decay and don't get enough fluoride in drinking water. Fluoride rinses and fluoride in toothpaste also help fight cavities.
common_complications: Fluoride is safe and effective when used properly. At high doses, it is toxic and may cause nausea. It is very difficult to receive toxic doses because home products use such small amounts of fluoride.

name: Inlays and Onlays
description: A dental inlay or onlay is used to restore a damaged or decayed tooth. An inlay is similar to a filling, but it lies within the cusps (bumps) on the chewing surface of the tooth. An onlay is larger. It replaces one or more decayed cusps. Dental inlays and onlays can be made of gold, composite resin (plastic) or ceramics. A direct inlay or onlay can be placed in one visit. The dentist will remove any decay and shape the remaining tooth. The resin will be molded, hardened in the office, then cemented to the tooth. An indirect inlay or onlay is made in a laboratory. It requires two office visits. The tooth will get a temporary filling between visits.
common_complications: Inlays and onlays can come loose if the cement washes out or combines with saliva while it is being applied. After the procedure, it is important to brush, floss and visit the dentist regularly. Contact your dentist if the tooth is sensitive for more than a few days, if your bite feels different or if the inlay or onlay becomes loose or falls out.

name: Recontouring
description: Dental recontouring is performed to change the length, shape or surface of a tooth. Recontouring can correct minor cosmetic imperfections or small areas where plaque or tartar are likely to build up. X-rays may be taken to determine if the tooth's enamel is thick enough to withstand recontouring. To recontour the tooth, the dentist will use a sanding disk or fine diamond burs to remove small amounts of tooth enamel. Usually an injection of local anesthesia is not necessary.  Sandpaper may be used to shape and smooth imperfections between teeth. After reshaping is complete, the teeth will be polished.
common_complications: Recontouring does not pose any major risks. The tooth may become sensitive if the enamel is thin after recontouring. Contact your dentist if the teeth become sensitive enough to bother you.

name: Apicoectomy
description: An apicoectomy may be needed when an infection develops in the bone, under the tooth, after root canal treatment. This procedure can fix the problem about 90% of the time so the tooth doesn't need to be extracted. In an apicoectomy, the root tip, or apex, is removed along with the infected tissue. A filling is then placed to seal the end of the root. An apicoectomy is also called endodontic microsurgery because it is often done using an operating microscope. Most apicoectomies take 30 to 90 minutes. The length will depend on the location of the tooth and the complexity of the root structure. Most apicoectomies are done by a root canal specialist (endodontist).
common_complications: Some bruising, swelling and numbness may occur in the area for a few days after the surgery. They should disappear within two weeks. Stitches may need to be removed two to seven days after the procedure, or they may dissolve by themselves. The main risk is that 10% of the time the infection comes back. In that case, the tooth may need to be extracted. Other risks include possible infection or nerve damage. An apicoectomy usually lasts for the life of the tooth.

name: Dental Sealants
description: A sealant is a clear or tinted plastic protective coating for teeth that is used to prevent cavities. Sealants are painted onto the chewing surfaces of the back teeth (molars and premolars). These are the areas where most cavities form. Sealants cover the grooves and crevices on the tooth surface where food often gets caught. This prevents bacteria from growing in the grooves and crevices and causing cavities. In the past, sealants usually were used only in children. But adults who have a high risk of cavities also can get sealants. Not only are they very effective, they cost a lot less than filling cavities. Applying sealants is quick and painless. It can be done during a routine dental visit.
common_complications: Risks are very rare. Sealants can cause problems in people who are allergic to plastics or components of plastics. There has also been some concern about the possible harmful effects of bisphenol A (BPA). This chemical is found in some sealants. However, studies show that any release of BPA from sealants is very small and limited to the time right after they are applied. The American Dental Association (ADA) and the U.S. Food and Drug Administration have found that sealants are safe. Based on current research, the ADA says that any low level of BPA exposure from sealants "poses no known health threat".

name: Veneers
description: Veneers are thin shells of ceramic or resin materials that are bonded to the front parts of teeth. Veneers are used to correct cosmetic defects or the way that teeth come together. If most of the tooth remains, veneers can improve the look of the tooth without cutting it down enough to place a crown. Most veneers do require removal of a small amount of enamel (the outer coating of the teeth). Veneers look like natural teeth.  Porcelain veneers resist stains from coffee, tea or smoking better than resin veneers do. Resin veneers cost less, but they chip easily and don't last as long as ceramic veneers. Veneers require two or three dental visits.
common_complications: Biting fingernails, chewing on pens, or putting extreme pressure on the teeth can cause veneers to come off, break, or chip. The veneers may not exactly match the color of your other teeth, and they may fall off. Teeth also can become sensitive when enamel is removed.

name: Vital Pulpotomy
description: Vital pulpotomy usually is done in children when decay in a tooth has reached the crown part of the pulp, but the pulp in the root of the tooth is still healthy. The pulp contains the tooth's nerve. The procedure also is done when the pulp is exposed as a result of injury or trauma. The affected part of the pulp (in the crown) can be removed, leaving the healthy part of the pulp in the root. A successful vital pulpotomy relieves sensitivity and pain.  It also allows tooth roots to continue to develop into mature roots.
common_complications: The area may be sore for a short time after the procedure. Vital pulpotomy has a high success rate. If the tooth still hurts or the gums swell after a vital pulpotomy, root canal treatment may be needed.

name: Nitrous Oxide
description: Nitrous oxide (N2O) is commonly called "laughing gas." It relieves pain and anxiety during dental procedures. People first inhale 100% oxygen through a soft nosepiece or mask. Then nitrous oxide is slowly mixed in with the oxygen. Nitrous oxide usually starts to work in less than five minutes. Nitrous oxide relaxes you but does not put you to sleep. You can still respond to your dentist's requests and answer questions. Your speech may be slightly slurred, and your responses may be slower than usual. Nitrous oxide is very safe when used by a properly trained dentist.
common_complications: Side effects may include headache, nausea or vomiting. Tell your dentist right away about any discomfort or anxiety you feel or concerns you have. Your motor skills and attention can be affected for as long as 15 minutes after you stop breathing the nitrous oxide. Pregnant women should avoid nitrous oxide. People with stuffy noses or breathing problems cannot receive this form of anesthesia. If you are a recovering substance abuser, speak to your drug counselor or psychiatrist about receiving nitrous oxide.  The euphoric feeling that nitrous oxide gives may be harmful to your recovery.

name: Local Anesthesia
description: Local anesthesia is medicine that is injected into the gum or inner cheek to numb part of the mouth. Lidocaine is the most common local anesthetic that dentists use. There are many others. They all have names ending in "-caine." Novocain is not used anymore because other drugs last longer, work better and are less likely to cause allergic reactions. An injection of local anesthesia can last up to several hours. After leaving the dentist's office, it may be difficult to speak clearly or eat for a while.
common_complications: Try to avoid eating while your lip and cheek are numb.  You could bite yourself and not even feel it. Side effects to local anesthesia are very rare. One possible side effect is a hematoma. This is a blood-filled swelling that can form when the injection needle hits a blood vessel. Also, the numbing medicine sometimes causes numbness outside of the targeted area. If this happens, the eyelid or mouth can droop. This will stop when the drug wears off. The needle can also injure a nerve, which can lead to numbness and pain for several weeks or months. The nerve usually heals over time.

name: Root Canal Treatment
description: The pulp, found in the center of the tooth, runs the entire length of the tooth inside the root canal. Pulp contains nerves and blood vessels. Root canal treatment (endodontic therapy) involves the removal of the pulp. Then the root canal is sterilized and filled with an inert material (gutta percha). This procedure is done when infection occurs in a tooth that has a deep cavity or when the pulp is injured by trauma. Afterward, the tooth is restored with a filling or crown. A general dentist or specialist (endodontist) will perform this procedure. Root canal treatment often can save a tooth from being extracted.
common_complications: The tooth may be sore or sensitive for two to three days after the procedure. Other possible complications include infection or puncturing a hole in the side of the tooth. After about 10% of root canal procedures, symptoms do not go away. The reason may be continuing infection or canal blockage. Treatment may require another root canal procedure or a type of surgery called an apicoectomy.

name: Dental Implants
description: Implants are devices made of titanium that replace the roots of missing teeth. They are used to support crowns, bridges or dentures. Implants are placed using local anesthesia and sometimes sedation. In most cases, placing a single dental implant requires less than one hour. The dentist drills a hole in the jawbone, inserts the implant and stitches the gums back into place. The second step comes three to six months later, after the implant has fused with the jawbone. The dentist cuts open the gum and inserts a metal cap into the implant. The crown, bridge or denture is added two to three weeks later, after the gums have healed around the cap. Some newer implants can be placed in only one step. Implants can be inserted only in someone who has healthy gums and enough bone in the jaw to hold the implant.
common_complications: Complications can include bleeding, infection, and injury to the nerves, sinuses, or nasal cavity. Implant surgery is successful more than 90% of the time. Occasionally, an implant fails to integrate with the surrounding bone. This is more likely to happen with smokers. Implants also can break or fail because of an infection. A "failed" implant has to be removed. Another implant can be placed right away or at a later visit.
